Code review · 7 November 2026 · v0.5.116 · 42d3def

Arke Studio Simplification Review

Arke Studio is fourteen weeks old and already 386,000 lines of TypeScript. Ten parallel reviews of its code, its performance and its user journeys produced the findings below. The largest costs come from three habits. The app rereads the whole world or its whole history on every save, message and finished job, on the Electron main thread. It writes the same glue by hand in hundreds of places, where the copies drift. And it builds one idea several times over, so people meet it in several forms. Most of the fixes are small, and every deliberate safety rule stays as it is.

Summary

The design underneath is careful. Reviewers repeatedly asked to keep the acceptance gate, the flush order of the journals, the world-ownership checks, the authenticated transport, prices before spend and the crash-recoverable action lifecycle. What has accumulated around them is the residue of an extraordinary pace: 5,184 commits since 31 July, about 370 a week.

Performance. The runtime cost is dominated by rereading, not by writing. An authored change rescans the whole world afterwards (131 gate operations, only 2 of which opt out), one chat message triggers four or five full rescans, each finished job reparses the app ledger three or four times plus the job journal, and start-up rereads the same history several times over. Measured on synthetic worlds, a commit that writes nothing takes about 0.9 s and 6,200 file reads, and a 5,000-job history stretches coordinator start-up from 0.23 s to 3.2 s. All of it runs on Electron's main thread, so the window and IPC stall with it. The fixes are incremental readers and indexes, a scan cache and the cheaper primitives issue 1840 already introduced. None of them touches the flush rules, which cost about half a millisecond per append.

Code. coordinator.ts is 25,158 lines, and one private method of 14,146 lines is the only implementation of 556 client commands. The glue around each command (world check, refresh, reply, error) is written by hand 477 times and has drifted: a stale command can rename the wrong world. The file still grows by about 1,200 lines a week after the placement rule, and 29% of main-line commits touch it. The same pattern shows in the client: 46 hand-rolled dialogs beside three shared ones, a reducer duplicated in the coordinator and already drifting, 395 CSS rules that can never match, and whole flows kept alive only by tests.

Journeys. Worldbuilding and production are well guarded where money or the world's content is at stake. The last mile is the least consistent part of the product: Export sits on seven screens under five labels, four sheets make the same Arke Player package and only one offers Submit, each production kind builds its own home and its own idea of what comes next, and the desktop and phone page lists disagree. The reviewers' proposed journeys roughly halve the step counts while keeping every price confirmation and acceptance decision.

Development loop. CI ran 744 times in the week to 7 November, 60,299 runner-minutes against a ceiling of 20 concurrent jobs, so jobs waited a median 18 minutes to start and the slowest tenth more than 3.5 hours. It also does not gate: 95% of merged pull requests merged about three minutes after their run started, only 23 of 303 pushes to main were verified green, and failures repeated across neighbouring branches used 45% of the week's runner-minutes. Type-checking builds eleven programs that each re-check the same contracts source; one combined program does the same work in 137 s instead of 483 s.

Fix first. The reviews turned up a handful of plain bugs that need no strategy: the wrong-world rename (CC-02), Edit on a location or faction landing on the world picker (UJ-01), no way to create a faction on desktop (UJ-02), a screen crash when the connection drops during audiobook requests (CS-03), a 64,000-token cap for local models that silently stopped applying (CH-05), and Story structure being unreachable on desktop (UP-06).

The moves that matter most

Ordered by payoff against effort and risk. Each links to the evidence.

  1. Fix the bugs the reviews confirmedUser journeyEffort SLow risk

    Each is small and verified by reading the code, and three were reproduced. Make refreshWorldSnapshot refuse a world that is not open, add the two missing edit routes, give Factions a desktop New button, hoist the conditional hook in BookRequests and turn on the Rules of Hooks lint rule, restore the local-model context cap, and give Story structure a desktop entry.

    CC-02 UJ-01 UJ-02 CS-03 CH-05 UP-06 UJ-05 UJ-06
  2. Stop rescanning the world after reads and operational writesPerformanceEffort MMedium risk

    Move chat reads and conversation writes to the primitives issue 1840 introduced for world open, pass finalWrite: "commit" where the last write already refreshed the bundle, and file each audiobook block in one commit. Then add an identity-keyed scan cache. On the large synthetic world a commit falls from about 0.9 s to an estimated 0.15 to 0.25 s, and a chat message loses four or five full scans.

    CH-01 RP-01 PM-02 CH-02 CH-06
  3. Read each journal once and keep an index in memoryPerformanceEffort MMedium risk

    One shared incremental reader for the job journal, the ledger and the change log, advanced on append, replaces full rereads per finished job, per world change and at start-up. Before that lands, four small changes take most of the cost away: skip the production-spend pass for worlds without video, compact the provider-call store with hysteresis, stop rebuilding index tables nothing reads, and pre-filter change-log records before validating them. The flush order is untouched.

    RP-02 CC-03 PM-01 PM-09 RP-03 RP-04 RP-06 CT-04
  4. Make CI a real gate, and cheaper to runPerformanceEffort MMedium risk

    Check all Node workspaces as one TypeScript program and the client as a second (356 s to about 90 s in CI), widen the two expressions that cost a quarter of the coordinator check, clear the client store's 15-second timer between test files, and build the client once. Then run fewer, fuller jobs and skip coordinator shards on client-only changes, which saves roughly 8,500 to 15,000 runner-minutes a week. Once the queue is short, make the checks required with auto-merge, so a breakage stops at one branch instead of fanning out.

    BT-01 BT-02 BT-03 BT-04 BT-05 BT-06
  5. Re-render only what an event changedPerformanceEffort SLow risk

    Five shared hooks and the picture tile subscribe to the whole store, so one unrelated event re-renders 71 to 86% of a screen. One-line selector changes cut the per-event cost on a 2,000-item shelf by 77 to 92% in Chrome. Narrow the root chat provider too, and add a ratchet on whole-store subscriptions so the gain holds.

    CS-01 CS-02 CS-06 CS-10 CS-11
  6. Send phones less, and let them cache itPerformanceEffort SLow risk

    The remote gateway sends the 7 MB app uncompressed with no-store, even for content-hashed files. Gzip and year-long caching of hashed assets alone take a throttled cold open from 6.58 s to 2.18 s, and repeat opens skip the transfer. Then mark contracts side-effect free, lazy-load routes and the 3D stage (about 48% less start-up script), and resume reconnects by collection instead of resending a large world's 17 MB.

    CS-04 CT-01 CS-05 RP-08 CT-03
  7. Put a ratchet on every rule that mattersSimplificationEffort SLow risk

    The placement rule for coordinator.ts did not stop its growth, the start-up chunk grew 9.4 times since August with nothing to flag it, and nothing stops new hand-rolled dialogs, raw font sizes or whole-store subscriptions. Counts that may only go down, in the existing lint scripts, plus a bundle-size budget and type-checking for the tests three workspaces leave out, cost about a day in total and stop regrowth while the larger work proceeds.

    CC-08 BT-08 CU-06 CU-10 CS-11 CS-03 BT-10
  8. Split the command switch, one domain per pull requestSimplificationEffort LMedium risk

    First give tests a public, typed dispatch() so a move fails at compile time instead of at run time. Then route commands through a small typed router that declares each command's world scope once and supplies reply and failure helpers. Domain modules then absorb the switch one domain at a time: 156 of the 237 members it touches belong to a single domain. A job port and a finalizer table do the same for the queue wiring and the 517-line filing chain.

    CC-07 CC-01 CC-02 CC-10 CC-04 CC-09 PM-04 PM-10
  9. Give every production one Publish page and one Arke Player sheetUser journeyEffort MMedium risk

    Build it from components that already exist, drive one export sheet by kind, and put Submit beside every finished package. The book route to its Arke Player package drops from three or four presses to two, five export labels become one, and 300 to 500 duplicated client lines go. On the coordinator side, one package writer replaces five exporters' staging and double hashing.

    UP-01 UP-02 UP-10 PM-08
  10. One definition for each navigation list, creation flow and homeUser journeyEffort MLow risk

    Render the desktop rail and the phone strip from one page list, give each screen one canonical address with a single redirect table, drive the four creation doors and the five sheet kinds from tables, and share one next-step contract between production homes. This removes the drift that hid Story structure and gave Overview three meanings.

    UP-06 UP-05 UP-09 UP-04 UJ-10 UJ-07

    Publish the reply before preparing proposal cards, start the founding summary during the build instead of in front of the first message, name conversations after the first turn, and scope the 96,000-character action guide to the thread. Streaming the reply is the larger step and needs a design check against the rule that a turn lands whole.

Cross-cutting themes

Patterns that more than one reviewer found independently. Each theme names the findings it draws on.

Work that grows with history runs on every operation

Four reviewers found the same shape independently. After an authored change the world store rescans every record file, the change log and every conversation log, and 129 of 131 gate operations rescan again at the end. Chat reads still pay that rescan. Each finished job reparses the app ledger three or four times and often the whole job journal and Bench history. Hellos and world opens reparse up to 32 MB of change log to find export rows. The provider-call store rewrites its whole file on every call once it holds 2,000 calls, and start-up rebuilds index tables nothing reads.

The journals' flush rules are not the cost: an appendFlushed row measured about 0.5 ms. The cost is reading everything again around it. Incremental readers advanced on append, a scan cache keyed by file identity, and the operational-write primitive from issue 1840 remove most of it without changing what is written or when it is synced.

Draws on RP-01 RP-02 CH-01 CH-02 CH-06 PM-01 PM-02 PM-09 CC-03 CC-12 RP-03 RP-04 RP-06 CT-04 RP-09 UP-03 RP-11 RP-14

The coordinator shares the window's thread

Desktop main builds the studio host in-process, so every synchronous pass in the coordinator also blocks Electron's main thread: window events, IPC and every renderer request that passes through a main-thread hook. The measured passes (rescans, full journal parses, the pure-JavaScript PNG codec, ffmpeg work held inside the world write gate) range from a few hundred milliseconds to several seconds.

The near-term answer is to remove the large passes described in the first theme and add yield points to long loops. Moving the PNG codec to a worker and doing media work before entering the gate are small. Moving the coordinator into a utility process is the structural option, worth taking only if stalls remain, and it needs a check against SPEC-001 D2.

Draws on RP-05 PM-11 PM-03 PM-08 CC-03 PM-01

Glue written by hand drifts

Where a rule is applied by convention at every call site, the copies have diverged. The world check appears 210 times with at least fifteen refusal messages, and 88 handlers skip it, which is how a stale command renamed the wrong world. Reply plumbing is copied into each handler and many failures are swallowed. Eleven hand-written harness loops have different stop and timeout rules. Fifteen canonical-JSON functions behave in at least three ways, including a pair that must produce the same digest on both sides of the wire. The client and the coordinator fold the same 46 events with two copies of the reducer, and one arm has already drifted.

The repository already has the tables these need: CLIENT_COMMAND_METADATA classifies all 556 commands and productionShape centralises production kinds. Extending them to own world scope, replies, finalizers and target kinds turns conventions into declarations the compiler checks.

Draws on CC-02 CC-10 CC-04 CH-08 CH-09 CT-05 CT-06 CS-09 PM-04 PM-10 CC-09 CT-07 PM-13 PM-14 PM-15

Rules without ratchets do not hold

The 5 September rule to follow domain modules before adding to coordinator.ts lowered the file's share of the code but not its growth: about 1,200 lines a week since, roughly 45 per new command. The Rules of Hooks lint rule is off, and one violation crashes a screen. Nothing counts hand-rolled overlays, raw font sizes or whole-store subscriptions, so each cleanup can regrow behind it.

The repository already runs eight policy scripts before oxlint. A count that may only go down, added to those scripts, is the cheapest durable guard available: about fifteen lines each.

Draws on CC-08 CU-06 CU-10 CS-03 CS-11 CC-07

One idea, built several times, met several ways

Duplication in the code shows up as inconsistency on screen. The same Arke Player package comes from four sheets with different contents. Export lives on seven screens under five labels. Production homes compute the next step five ways. There are four creation patterns for productions and four for sibling world entities, three download-progress renderers, four ways of asking about spend and four chat entry points. Underneath, 46 surfaces hand-roll dialogs and popovers, five sites re-implement voice-upload consent, and two review bars are the same code renamed.

Consolidating these is where code simplification and journey simplification are the same piece of work, and the reviewers' step counts show the gain: most proposed journeys are about half as long.

Draws on UP-01 UP-02 UP-09 UP-04 UJ-10 UJ-14 UP-08 UJ-13 UP-12 CU-01 CU-04 CU-13 UP-07 UJ-11

Dead paths stay green

Tests that render components directly keep retired features passing after their last entry point has gone. The whole Propose-timing flow has had no caller since Audio Studio replaced the Timing view, yet its tests pass. The film door's second step has been unreachable since 8 September, with 77 lines of tests. The first-run screen is reachable from nowhere and is the only place two start-up warnings appear. 395 CSS rules can never match, three events are never emitted, and the local-model context cap disappeared with the retired harness while the documentation still describes it.

Testing through routes and entry points where possible, and a periodic dead-surface scan (the reviewers' scripts are a starting point), would catch these as they happen.

Draws on CU-02 CU-03 UP-04 UJ-08 CT-08 CH-05 UP-05 UJ-01

Phones pay for everything twice

Remote access is a headline feature, and the network is where it hurts. Every visit downloads the 7 MB app shell uncompressed and uncached. Every reconnect resends the whole world, about 17 MB for a large one. The client then re-validates frames the coordinator already validated, on a slower CPU. Compression and immutable caching of hashed assets, collection-level resume and validating once at the source together change the phone experience more than any single client optimisation.

Draws on CS-04 RP-08 CS-05 CT-03 CT-01 RP-07

Waiting without being told

Several waits and failures are silent. A chat reply stays invisible until validation, card preparation and two refreshes finish, and the first message in a newly founded world waits for a summary of the founding transcript without saying so. A command that fails its schema gets no reply at all. In Form mode a refused world creation shows nothing. Onboarding's second primary action skips the downloads the person chose without a word.

Surfacing these costs little, and in most cases the existing toaster or progress label is already there to use.

Draws on CH-03 CH-07 CT-07 CC-10 UJ-05 UJ-06 CH-11

The development loop is the bottleneck

With hundreds of agent pull requests a week, the cost of every check is multiplied. A green CI run is 21 jobs and 152 runner-minutes, two thirds of them on Windows, and the runners are full: work waits longer in the queue than it takes to run. Merges do not wait for CI, so one broken base fails dozens of neighbouring branches. Inside a run, type-checking repeats the contracts source eleven times, two expressions cost a quarter of the coordinator check, and twenty client test files idle up to 20 seconds on a timer. Each test process also pays 0.5 s to evaluate the whole contracts package and its 36,700 schemas.

The contributor guides add the human half of the same cost: the testing guide and the code map together run to 58,000 words of prepend-only notes, and the format script would rewrite 2,496 hand-formatted files if anyone ran it. Most of the remedies are configuration, not code.

Draws on BT-01 BT-02 BT-03 BT-04 BT-05 BT-06 BT-09 BT-10 BT-13 BT-14 CT-01 CC-07

Roadmap

The order matters more than the dates. The first fortnight fixes the bugs, takes the cheapest performance wins and puts guards in place so the cleanup holds. The quarter's structural work then lands in small, separately reviewable steps. Each item names the findings it draws on; effort and risk are the reviewers' estimates for someone who knows the area.

User journeys

The two journey reviewers rebuilt sixteen journeys from the routes, navigation calls, buttons and conditions in the code. A step is one navigation, action, decision, wait or setting. These are readings of the code, not observed sessions: they describe the path the code allows, without errors or slow providers. The proposed journeys keep the price confirmations and acceptance decisions the reviewers marked as deliberate.

Coordinator · CC · 13 findings

The coordinator's core and the coordinator.ts monolith

coordinator.ts is a 25,158-line file whose single Coordinator class holds 183 state fields and 257 methods. One private method, handleClientMessageInner, is 14,146 lines long and contains a 556-case switch that is the only implementation of most client commands. The code mostly delegates to domain modules, but the glue around each call (open-world guard, snapshot refresh, reply event, error copy) is written by hand 477 times and has drifted: 88 handlers skip the world check, and a probe showed a stale command renaming the wrong world and switching the open world back. Splitting it up is practical, because 156 of the 237 members the switch touches belong to a single domain, so per-domain command modules behind a small typed router can absorb the switch one domain per PR. The file still grows by about 1,200 lines a week after the 2026-09-05 placement rule and appears in 29% of main-line commits. The biggest performance item in this slice is that every snapshot refresh and every finished job re-reads the whole ledger, job journal and Bench history on the Electron main process.

How this area is built, and how it was reviewed

Hosts (desktop main.ts, dev.ts, node-studio-host.ts) call createStudioHost. That builds a Coordinator from 80 options and wraps its serverApplication in a StudioServer, which owns the authenticated WebSocket Transport. Transport validates each frame with ClientMessageSchema.parse and calls onMessage. That calls handleClientMessage, which counts in-flight commands and turns a thrown error into a generic command.failed, and then handleClientMessageInner. A 58-line prologue applies per-kind policies from hard-coded kind lists: background world store, founding-decision and Bench serialisation, genesis review reset, and adapter interception. Then one switch (msg.kind) over 556 kinds runs, ending in a never exhaustiveness check.

A typical case gets the open store, compares its world id with msg.worldId, calls a domain function (gate/, productions/, bench/, world-chat/ …) that persists through the world store or a flushed journal, then calls refreshWorldSnapshot or broadcastSnapshot and emits a correlated result or refusal event.

State reaches clients two ways. emit(event) validates with DomainEventSchema, folds into the pure ReadModel, appends to the unflushed change log unless the type is on a deny-list, broadcasts, and triggers side effects (spend projection, diagnostics, conversation reconciliation). Direct ReadModel setters followed by a snapshot broadcast are the other path.

Long-running work is tracked in about 28 AbortController registers. getInitialEvents replays them to new windows and stopApplication aborts them. Finished jobs are filed by onJobTerminal. Around the class sit studio-server.ts (host adapter), application/ (an engine layer re-exported as @arke-studio/engine, of which the coordinator uses six calls), read-model.ts (79-case fold), supervisor.ts (generic child supervisor) and world-provider.ts (an interface with 19 optional members).

Scope and method

Read CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, packages/coordinator/AGENTS.md, the code-map rows for commands and acceptance, and the four earlier audits in docs/code-analysis. Parsed coordinator.ts, contracts frames.ts and events.ts and the coordinator test files with the TypeScript parser (parse only, no type information) to list class members, the command switch, the contract unions, this.* coupling per case, and the private members tests reach through casts. Members and cases were classified into 18 domains by name. This is a heuristic, and the scripts and outputs are saved beside this file (members.cjs, switch.cjs, classify.cjs, coupling.cjs, responsibility-map.txt/.json).

Measured: git history (weekly sizes on main, commit and merge hotspots, extraction commits); a traced tsc --extendedDiagnostics --generateTrace of the coordinator.ts import graph; tsx import cost and Coordinator construction time; zod cost of event validation and of the spend reader's row parsing. Two behaviour probes ran in a scratch app root (a stale rename-world and a stale reorder-episodes); the working tree was unchanged before and after.

Not covered: the internals of the domain folders, client store.ts, transport and snapshot runtime cost, and timings on Windows (all owned by other reviewers or not measurable here). I did not run the package's full typecheck or test suite, and I could not read the private specs, so SPEC citations are quoted from code comments only.

Decomposition plan

  1. Pin the seamsLow risk+80 src; ~300 test lines edited

    Add a public awaitable dispatch(msg) and a typed test seam to Coordinator; codemod the 92 casting test files. Add the lint ratchet as a warning (CC-07, CC-08). No production behaviour change.

    Every later step then fails at compile time rather than test run time. Do it in one PR when few branches are open; it touches 92 test files.

  2. Close the world-scope hazardMedium risk~40 changed

    refreshWorldSnapshot no longer switches worlds (or a new refreshOpenWorld replaces its 171 msg.worldId uses). loadWorldOnce short-circuits the open world. The stale-rename probe becomes a test (CC-02 B, CC-12 B).

    A small behaviour change, and it fixes a verified bug. Check refusal-versus-ignore against SPEC-002 and SPEC-001 §2.5.

  3. Shared infrastructure inside the classLow risk~-400 net

    RunRegistry for the 28 registers; one KeyedSerializer; productionOf and chapterOf helpers; settings cache; reply and fail helpers as private methods that already have the router context's shape (CC-04, CC-10, CC-11).

    A redesign of helpers but mechanical at call sites. Keep replay order and abort semantics; run studio-lifecycle, shutdown-race and the audiobook replay tests.

  4. Extract workflow servicesMedium risk~1,700 moved

    export-cut to productions/export-cut.ts; narrateSection, narrateVoicedPage and resolveProse to a read-aloud service; conversationActionDependencies to world-chat/; makeBenchPicture to bench/; readAudiobookChapter, castChapterVoices and runIllustration to productions/audiobook-runs.ts (CC-13).

    Mechanical, following the 2026-09-14 precedent. Constructor arguments replace this. Move shared piece and chunk state together.

  5. Router, context and the small domainsMedium risk~2,500 moved; +400 router and context

    Create commands/router.ts and commands/context.ts with the exhaustiveness type; turn the prologue kind lists into declared policies; move setup/onboarding/updates, recovery/diagnostics, audio studio/drama/music, comic, genesis/founding and world lifecycle (~6 modules).

    The router starts with the old switch as its fallback for every kind not yet moved, so each PR moves one domain and the rest keep working. Serialisation order must stay identical.

  6. The large domains, one PR eachMedium risk~17,000 moved

    Settings/providers/harness, voice, visual identity, authoring/gate, prose, publishing/exports, film, bench/takes/artifacts, World Chat/conversation actions, and audiobook (split into runs, records/pictures and read-aloud).

    Move case bodies verbatim with their single-domain helpers and fields (156 of the 237 members the switch touches are single-domain). Run that domain's tests, transport.test.ts and typecheck. No reformatting (house style).

  7. Job finalizersMedium risk~520 moved

    onJobTerminal becomes queue/finalizers.ts plus per-domain registrations, with one ledger lookup per job (CC-09).

    SPEC-009 crash model: keep throw-means-retry and the waiter ordering (SPEC-047 R-45).

  8. Lifecycle, composition and eventsMedium risk~2,000 moved; ~250 removed

    Constructor into composition builders; startApplication and stopApplication into application/lifecycle.ts; serveFile routes into media/routes.ts; event policy table; ManifestSource replaces the opts getter; dev.ts built on createNodeStudioHost (CC-05, CC-06).

    Startup and shutdown ordering are covered by studio-lifecycle, v2-launch and transport tests. Concrete harness imports stay in v2-launch.ts.

  9. Optional deeper redesignHigh riskvaries

    Incremental ledger and spend index (CC-03 A, can run in parallel at any time); uniform reply envelope or per-requester replies; routing of overlapping prose commands through the application/ engine.

    These change protocol or persistence semantics and need the persistence, client and contracts reviewers. The end state of steps 1-8 is coordinator.ts at about 1,500-2,500 lines (façade: dispatch, emit, start/stop) plus about 15 domain command modules of 250-3,000 lines each and infrastructure modules of 150-900 lines.

Where
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:7683
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:7741
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:21826
  • packages/contracts/src/frames.ts:163
  • packages/coordinator/src/arke-actions/registry.ts:215
Evidence
  • handleClientMessageInner spans coordinator.ts:7683-21828 (14,146 lines, 56% of the file). Its switch (msg.kind) (7741-21825) has 556 case labels in 477 groups. That matches the 556 options of ClientMessageSchema (frames.ts:163) exactly, and the switch is closed by const unhandled: never = msg (21826).
  • Case sizes run from a median of 19 lines and p90 of 64 to a maximum of 427 (export-cut). 250 groups are 20 lines or fewer.
  • The 58-line prologue (7683-7740) applies policies from hard-coded lists naming 54 kinds: background world store (9 kinds), founding-decision serialisation (20), Bench take and dispatch fences (4 and 14), genesis review reset (10), and adapter interception. It re-enters handleClientMessage with six positional flags, such as benchTakeActionHeld and audiobookStore.
  • Each domain is scattered across the file. Audiobook code sits in 19 separate regions between lines 1538 and 22394, World Chat in 22, and settings in 24 (responsibility-map.txt).
  • Coupling stays local. The switch touches 237 distinct this.* members: 156 are used by one domain only, and 200 by at most two. Only 17 are used by five or more domains: opts, emit, nowIso, refreshWorldSnapshot, transport, appLog, appSettings, jobQueue, stopping, readModel, stillOpen, trackBackground, voiceService, enqueueBatch, refreshIfStillOpen, rejectEnqueue and sessionInput.
  • A table keyed by kind already exists: CLIENT_COMMAND_METADATA (registry.ts:215) classifies all 556 kinds, with compile-time parity (registry.ts:1835-1841).
Why it matters

Each new command adds a case to the same method, so the method is the place where unrelated features collide. Commands that share a domain sit hundreds or thousands of lines apart. Cross-cutting rules (world scope, serialisation, reply shape) live in the prologue's kind lists and in each case's own copy, and the compiler cannot check them. The 2026-08-04 architecture audit (AR-1) asked for a public command facade. The transport was split out afterwards (studio-server.ts), but dispatch is still one private method, which is why tests reach into it through casts (CC-07).

Options
  1. APer-domain command modules behind a small typed routerRecommended

    Create src/commands/ with a router, a CommandContext and one module per domain. The context holds the 17 widely shared members plus requireWorld, reply and fail. Each module exports its kind list as const and a handle(msg, ctx) with its own switch over that subset. A type-level check in the style of registry.ts's _EveryClientCommandIsClassified proves the lists cover every kind exactly once. The prologue's lists become declared per-kind policies applied by the router (serializeBy, backgroundStore, resetsGenesisReview). Move case bodies verbatim, one domain per PR, taking their single-domain helpers and fields along. Each switch stays small (10-80 kinds), so narrowing stays cheap and no mapped type over the whole union is needed.

  2. BA flat handler-per-kind registry beside CLIENT_COMMAND_METADATA

    One entry per command next to its metadata. However, a mapped type over all 556 kinds is what registry.ts already spends about 15 s of check time on, and the code there notes TS2590 (registry.ts:1818-1822). Handler files would still need grouping by domain.

  3. CKeep the switch and replace each body with a call

    case labels stay in coordinator.ts and each body becomes return handleX(msg, ctx). This is the smallest change and the natural first increment of A. On its own it leaves about 1,500 lines of routing, and every new command still edits the hotspot.

Impact

Moves about 14,000 switch lines (13,958 in case bodies) and about 7,500 lines of domain-named helper methods out of coordinator.ts, estimated from the responsibility map. End state: coordinator.ts at about 1,500-2,500 lines plus about 15 domain modules of 250-3,000 lines each. Merge contention spreads from one file touched by 29% of main-line commits to per-domain files. No runtime gain is claimed, and type-check time moves rather than disappears (coordinator.ts's own check is about 10.3 s today).

Risk

Verbatim moves keep behaviour, but this inside arrow callbacks and closures must be rebound to the context or a domain object. The prologue's serialisation order must stay identical; the bench shutdown-race, genesis-wiring, single-act and dispatch-refusal tests cover it. 92 test files reach private members through unchecked casts, so do CC-07 first, or a move fails at test run time rather than at compile time. Check against SPEC-001 §2.6 (sequenced frames and read model).

CC-02Hand-written world checks have drifted: a stale command can change the wrong world and switch the open oneSimplificationUser journeyEffort MMedium riskHigh confidence
Where
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:10019
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:12410
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:24901
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:24828
  • packages/coordinator/src/world/provider.ts:454
  • packages/coordinator/src/transport.ts:331
Evidence
  • store.worldId !== msg.worldId appears 210 times on 208 lines, with at least 15 different refusal messages and five main reactions: 132 silent returns, 33 custom blocks, 24 thrown Errors, 10 answer callbacks, 2 thrown refusals and 7 others.
  • 420 of the 556 command kinds carry a required worldId (counted from ClientMessageSchema.options). Yet 88 case groups use the open store and msg.worldId without ever comparing them. Examples: rename-world (10019), reorder-episodes (12410), restore-bible, delete-scene (11478), set-trim (13557), bench-keep and bench-accept.
  • refreshWorldSnapshot(worldId) (24901) calls provider.loadWorld(worldId). When the ids differ, that closes the open store and opens the other world (world/provider.ts:454-466). It is called 194 times, 171 of them with msg.worldId. The code already warns about this beside refreshIfStillOpen (24828): 'that loads the world it is given … the old one reopened underneath it'.
  • Probe (stale-world-probe.mts, scratch app root holding fixture world A and a new world B): after open-world B, a rename-world naming A renamed B and left A open. A failing reorder-episodes naming A also switched the open world back to A. Neither switch emitted world.opened.
  • Stale ids are realistic. Messages a reconnecting device sent before its hello are replayed after it (transport.ts:331), and paired phones share the one coordinator.
Why it matters

A person or a paired device can rename or edit the world they are no longer looking at. The app can also quietly jump every window back to a previous world. The root cause is structural: the world rule is re-typed in each handler, so it is easy to miss and impossible to check centrally.

Options
  1. AEnforce a declared world scope once in the routerRecommended

    Give each kind with worldId a scope. The default is the open world only; the 9 background-store kinds in the prologue list work on any world through withBackgroundWorldStore; open, archive, browse and borrow commands are cross-world. The router checks the scope before the handler runs and answers a mismatch the same way every time, as command.failed with the request id or as a typed refusal. This deletes about 210 guard lines.

  2. BStop refresh from switching worlds (immediate)

    Make refreshWorldSnapshot return early, or emit command.failed, when the open store is not worldId, and prefer refreshIfStillOpen(store) wherever a store is in hand. One method changes, and the silent world switch goes away for all 171 callers. Wrong-world writes in handlers that skip the guard remain until A.

  3. CAudit and patch the 88 handlers individually

    This fixes today's cases but leaves the pattern free to drift again with the next command.

Impact

Fixes a verified wrong-world write and a silent world switch. The switch is reachable from the 57 handlers that refresh with msg.worldId and have no guard, out of the 88 that skip it. B is about 10 lines and takes under a day; A removes about 210 guard lines and makes the rule checkable. Either one also drops a scan of the worlds folder from each refresh (CC-12).

Risk

A stale command that today silently reloads the named world would be refused instead. I found no flow that relies on refresh to open a world (open and create use openWorld). Background-store kinds must keep working on a world that is not open. Check against SPEC-002 (world access) and SPEC-001 §2.5 (remote devices) to decide whether a stale command should be refused or ignored. Turn the probe into a regression test.

Evidence
  • setDisplayWorld (4820), which every refreshWorldSnapshot calls, runs scheduleProductionSpend (4826). That calls readProductionSpend (spend/read.ts:21).
  • readProductionSpend reads ledger.jsonl and queue/jobs.jsonl whole, runs JSON.parse and a zod parse on every row in one synchronous loop (evidenceFile, read.ts:8), then reads every Bench session's events.jsonl in the open world.
  • emit also schedules this pass for ledger.appended, spend.status, every bench.* event and terminal job.updated (4962-4963). Passes are coalesced to one in flight plus a dirty flag, so a busy run keeps them going back to back.
  • recordLedger (7422) reads the whole ledger again (spendLedgerRead) and runs detectDrift over it. The queue's runtime ledger.has does a strict full read and scan (3954). coordinator.ts has 16 more ledger.readAll().find(…) lookups by job id, 6 of them inside onJobTerminal.
  • The job journal appends a full job snapshot on every transition (queue/dispatcher.ts:564-567), and the ledger is never compacted (spend/ledger.ts:103). Both files grow for the life of the install.
  • Measured parse cost alone (fixture rows, Linux, spend-cost.mts), for the job journal plus the ledger: about 13 ms at 1,000 rows each, 146 ms at 10,000, and 521 ms at 50,000 per pass. File I/O and Bench events come on top.
  • The coordinator runs inside the Electron main process (coordinator package.json description).
  • The 2026-08-04 startup audit (ST-3, #128) asked for the ledger to be read once into a set. That was applied at queue startup (readJobIds) but not at runtime.
Why it matters

The cost grows with total history, not with the work in hand, and it lands on the same event loop that serves the window and the WebSocket. Heavy users, such as audiobook runs with thousands of jobs, pay it many times per job. The result is sluggish UI during long runs that gets worse month by month.

Options
  1. AIn-memory indexes advanced on append, with spend folded from eventsRecommended

    Seed a ledger index (by job id, with running totals) and a latest-row-by-job map once at startup. Advance them only after each confirmed flushed append. Fold production spend incrementally from the events that already pass through emit. The files remain the durable record and are re-read only on world open or after a failed read.

  2. BIncremental tail reads

    Remember the byte offset and parsed rows per file, parse only the appended bytes, and reset on truncation or a change of file identity. This is a smaller change with the same semantics and suits the append-only files.

  3. CCompute production spend only on demand

    Recompute only while a screen shows the figure, memoised by file size and mtime. This is cheap, but it leaves the per-job ledger reads in place.

Impact

Removes synchronous parsing proportional to history from every command refresh and every terminal job. At 10,000 rows per file each pass costs about 0.15 s. An audiobook run that finishes 2,000 jobs triggers several passes and ledger reads per job, which adds up to minutes of main-thread CPU over the run. This is an estimate: measured per-pass cost multiplied by passes per job, assuming history stays near 10,000 rows.

Risk

Keep the appendFlushed order (write, fsync, close, acknowledge). Keep the rule that an unreadable ledger means unknown, never empty (dedupeLedgerRead, SPEC-032 R-21). Never compact or rewrite the ledger (SPEC-009 R-16). The index must advance only after a confirmed append. This overlaps the persistence/runtime reviewer; agree one design.

Coordinator · PM · 15 findings

Production, generation and media pipelines in the coordinator, plus providers

Generation is already built on one shared substrate: a single durable job queue (queue/dispatcher.ts) submits, polls, verifies, lands and ledgers work for every production kind, so the per-kind run loops (audiobook, frame run, comic Make, drama, music) do not reimplement plan → dispatch → poll → accept, and a generic pipeline framework would add code rather than remove it. The simplification wins are narrower: one job port instead of seven ad hoc wirings, a mechanical split of the 2,987-line dispatcher, a registry for job target kinds (production kinds are already centralized in productionShape), shared export packaging and a handful of duplicated media helpers.

The biggest problems are performance costs that grow with history and run on the Electron main process: every finished job re-parses the whole app ledger three to four times and, through the production-spend projection, the whole job journal as well; every audiobook block costs three full world rescans (the repository's own Windows profile shows 1.29 s per block at 3,750 artifacts); take arrival and interactive export do heavy media work inside the world write gate. All of these can be fixed without touching the deliberate invariants (flushed appends, the outbox protocol, ownership checks).

How this area is built, and how it was reviewed

Every production kind generates media through one durable outbox. queue/dispatcher.ts (JobQueue) appends each job to the app-level queue/jobs.jsonl before any provider I/O and runs one FIFO lane per provider (two concurrent jobs by default, one for local engines). It submits through a DispatchClient from packages/providers. Every client is wrapped by capture.ts, which writes a flushed start record and a flushed finish record to calls.jsonl for each HTTP call. The queue polls every 1.5 s, saves completed bytes as hash-verified receipts, verifies the files and lands them in the world. It then appends one line per terminal outcome to ledger.jsonl (spend/ledger.ts) and hands the job to the coordinator's onJobTerminal.

Domain finalization turns landed media into immutable takes (takes/arrival.ts), artifacts (artifacts/filing.ts) or kind-specific records, and then probes the media (ffprobe), checks motion quality (ffmpeg QC) and draws posters.

Per-kind orchestration sits on top. The audiobook run (audiobook-run.ts, audiobook-book.ts) prices a chapter and enqueues one grouped speech request at a time. It awaits each request through JobWaiters, aligns the audio with local word timing, cuts it into block takes and checkpoints the chapter record after every block. The frame run is a durable cursor file advanced on terminal events. The comic Make card is an 87-line policy loop over injected operations. Audio drama uses single-job awaits; music uses cached local ffmpeg renders.

Exports have several writers: web packages, Arke Player ZIPs, manuscripts, and music, story and comic players. publications/ is the newer crash-safe edition-delivery framework, and publishing/ uploads editions to Aonik. Production kind is resolved once by contracts productionShape, while job behaviour branches on a free-string target.kind.

Scope and method

Read the production code in coordinator src/productions, queue, takes, media, audio, voice, comfyui, local-ai, artifacts, sheets, references, spend, publications and publishing, plus packages/providers and packages/voice (74,074 source lines). Traced the generation path end to end: enqueue → JobQueue → captured provider client → result receipt → landing → onJobTerminal → take arrival or artifact filing → ledger → spend projection. Counts come from git grep/wc; line references were checked by hand.

Measurements (synthetic, Linux container, Node 22.23; Windows I/O and process spawn will differ): full ledger and job-journal parse cost and the pure-JS PNG codec, with scripts kept in the review session; and the repository's own packages/coordinator/scripts/profile-audiobook-filing.ts, run with TMPDIR pointed at the scratch folder. The repository also documents a Windows run of the same profile (docs/development/audiobook-filing-profile.md, 2026-11-02), which is quoted where relevant.

Not covered: coordinator.ts beyond the places it wires this slice, world-chat, harness, persistence and transport internals (other reviewers). No tests were run and the app was not launched. Real provider latencies, Windows fsync and process-spawn costs, and ffmpeg run times were not measured. The SPEC-nnn documents are private and absent, so every recommendation that touches a cited requirement says what to check.

Earlier audits: the 2026-08-04 startup audit's ST-3 (superlinear queue recovery) was acted on. foldJobHistory folds history in one pass and recovery reads the ledger once into a set (dispatcher.ts:413, :2332). The runtime per-job dedupe is still a full ledger read (see PM-01). The 2026-09-05 documentation audit asked for a generation-to-take trace, and the code map now has "Generate media and receive a take". The other two audits do not touch this slice.

Evidence

ledger.jsonl and queue/jobs.jsonl are app-wide, append-only and never compacted. LedgerFile has no index: every read is readFile, then JSON.parse and LedgerEntrySchema.parse on every line. Tracing one terminal job:

  1. terminalize → appendLedgerOnce → ledger.has(job.id). Outside start-up recovery, this is wired as a full readAllStrict() followed by .some((e) => e.jobId === jobId) (coordinator.ts:3954). That is one full parse.
  2. The append goes to recordLedger, which flushes the line and then calls spendLedgerRead() → readAllChecked() to re-evaluate rolling spend and drift (coordinator.ts:7450). Second full parse.
  3. onJobTerminal finds the job's cost with (await this.ledger.readAll()).find(e => e.jobId === job.id) for shots, passes, voice lines, board sheets, bench takes, performances and reference tiles (7 sites, 6594-6825). Third full parse.
  4. Audiobook, hear and quote runs call actualCost, wired the same way at 2351, 11695, 15393 and 24024. Fourth full parse for those jobs.
  5. emit schedules scheduleProductionSpend() on every terminal job.updated, every ledger.appended, every spend.status and every bench.* event (4963). Each pass re-reads and zod-parses the whole ledger, the whole job journal and every .sessions/*/events.jsonl in the world (spend/read.ts:21-56), then broadcasts a full snapshot. Passes are coalesced to one running and one pending, and productionSpend only uses video productions with scenes (rollups.ts:67), yet the files are read first for every open world, including story, audiobook and music worlds.

Synthetic costs measured here: ledger 10 / 40 / 127 ms at 1k / 5k / 20k entries; job journal 133 / 363 ms at 1,000 / 3,000 grouped speech jobs (33 / 100 MB). The parse loops are synchronous, and the coordinator runs inside the Electron main process (apps/desktop/src/main.ts:218).

Why it matters

The cost of finishing one job grows with everything ever generated on the machine, so a heavy user's app gets slower the more it is used. Long audiobook and storyboard runs finish hundreds of jobs back to back, and each one stalls the main process (window, IPC and WebSocket) while history is re-parsed. The 2026-08-04 audit fixed the same pattern at start-up (ST-3), but it remains on the runtime hot path.

Options
  1. AGate and debounce the production-spend refreshRecommended

    Skip scheduleProductionSpend unless the open world has a production with scenes and video dispatch, and ignore events whose worldId is another world. Add a trailing 1-2 s debounce so a burst of finished jobs costs one pass. Small, local change; the projection's authority (journal + ledger + Bench logs) is unchanged.

  2. BTail-indexed readers for the two append-only filesRecommended

    Give LedgerFile an in-memory Map<jobId, entry> and entry list, built once and updated on each append (appends are already serialized by its WriteQueue). Revalidate by file size and mtime, and read only the bytes appended since the last offset; fall back to a full reload when the file shrinks, which is what the torn-tail repair does. has, entryFor(jobId) and readAllChecked answer from the index. has must still reject when the file is unreadable (R-16 dedupe), and unavailable must keep its R-21 meaning. Use the same tail reader for jobs.jsonl in spend/read.ts.

  3. CDerive production spend from in-memory queue state

    Build the projection from the queue's folded jobs plus a ledger index instead of from files. The projection needs tombstoned (deleted) jobs, which the queue drops when folding (dispatcher.ts:430), so this changes which component is the authority and needs a design decision. Not recommended first.

Impact

Per finished job today: 3-4 direct ledger parses plus 1-2 projection passes. Using the measured parse costs, that is about 0.3-0.5 s of synchronous main-process work with 5k ledger entries and 1k grouped jobs, and about 0.9-1.5 s with 20k entries and 3k jobs. After A, story, audiobook and music worlds skip the projection entirely. After B, each lookup is O(1) and each pass reads only new bytes, about 1 ms. Over a 600-request audiobook run that saves roughly 3-15 minutes of main-process CPU and removes the stalls of 100-400 ms per job. Arithmetic: measured parse costs × reads per job × jobs.

Risk

The dedupe read must stay strict: rejecting when the file is unreadable is what prevents duplicate ledger lines (comment at dispatcher.ts:217-224). The tail index must detect the torn-tail repair rewrite. Guard tests: coordinator test/queue/dispatcher.test.ts (ledger dedupe and crash window ⑦), test/spend/read.test.ts and rollups.test.ts, and the spend-status and drift tests. Check against SPEC-008 R-16, SPEC-009 R-16, SPEC-032 R-21, SPEC-008 R-13 and the lifetime production spend amendment (PR #2286).

Evidence

For each block, runAudiobookChapter does three writes:

  1. file() → fileGeneratedArtifact, a gate operation that commits the sidecar.
  2. measureInto, which runs ffprobe and then a second gate commit to add mediaInfo.
  3. keep() → updateAudiobook → writeOwned → store.ownedWrite, which checkpoints the chapter record.

Each write ends in WorldStore.rescan(), which calls scanWorld over the whole world even when it knows the changed paths. The regression test pins the count: "files, measures and checkpoints one cut with three scans" (audiobook-filing-scans.test.ts:11). Issue #1794 already cut it from five to three.

The repository's own Windows profile measured 11.0 s, 14.1 s and 38.7 s per 30 blocks at 0, 500 and 3,750 extra artifacts (367 ms → 1.29 s per block), with scans 54-86% of elapsed. My Linux rerun of the same script gave 315 / 500 / 1,200 ms per block at 0 / 500 / 2,000 artifacts, scans 76-87%.

Every kept take is itself an artifact, so the world grows as the book is read. The block's audio is also written two or three times (a level-adjusted temp WAV, then the artifact copy) and read back for hashing. ffprobe is spawned for 16-bit PCM WAVs, although every MediaInfo field it records (durationSec, hasAudio, audioChannels, audioSampleRateHz) is already in the WAV header the run has just parsed with readSpeechWav.

Why it matters

Filing time per block grows with world size, so reading a whole book gets slower as it goes: the cost is quadratic over the book. The filing profile doc notes that users reported 40-60 s gaps between saved blocks, and rescans are a measurable part of that. Three concurrent chapter readers did not finish faster (10.3 s versus 11.0 s at 0 artifacts) because the world gate serializes every commit.

Options
  1. AOne commit per blockRecommended

    Derive MediaInfo in JS for PCM WAV takes. For other formats, probe the source file before entering the gate and confirm its identity afterwards. Then write the media copy, the sidecar (with mediaInfo) and the chapter-record merge in one commit. A fileGeneratedBytes variant that takes the in-memory PCM avoids the temp WAV write, read and unlink. The checkpoint stays per block, so R-18's 'a stop leaves what was made standing' still holds.

  2. BOne commit per grouped request

    File every cut of one grouped request in a single commit. That means fewer commits again (a six-block request goes from 18 to 1), but a crash loses up to one request's cuts. The paid audio stays as a landed job that the next press adopts without paying again (priorGroupJob), so the loss is filing work, not money. Check SPEC-047 R-18 before choosing it.

  3. CMake rescans incremental (persistence reviewer)

    Have rescan(changedPaths) update the bundle incrementally instead of running scanWorld. This complements A, and on its own fixes every caller, but it belongs to the WorldStore owner.

Impact

A cuts rescans per block from 3 to 1 and drops one ffprobe spawn per WAV block. Using the Windows profile's slope (scan ≈ 66 ms + 0.081 ms per artifact), rescans for a 3,600-block book whose artifacts grow from zero fall from about 38 minutes to about 13. At 3,750 artifacts a block goes from 1.29 s to about 0.55 s. The arithmetic is the sum over blocks of scans per block × scan cost.

Risk

Filing identity and deduplication (generatedIdentity, restoring missing media), the per-chapter record lane (recordLanes) and the arrangement refusal must keep working. filing.ts:495-503 records why probing moved outside the gate; A keeps the probe outside. Update audiobook-filing-scans.test.ts to expect 1. Run the audiobook-grouped, audiobook and artifacts tests and the profile script. Check against SPEC-047 R-18 and SPEC-015 §2.3.

Evidence

recordTakesFromJob does all of its work inside store.gateOp(async () => { ... }) (arrival.ts:248). That gate serializes every world write and suppresses the watcher. Inside it:

  • a streaming SHA-256 of the clip (hashMedia, :269);
  • motion QC, an ffmpeg framemd5 run capped at QC_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000 (:275);
  • poster extraction, another ffmpeg run capped at POSTER_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000 (:281).

Both ffmpeg runs are wired in the shipped desktop (apps/desktop/src/main.ts:1377, take-qc.ts). After the gate, measureTake → measureProductionMedia hashes the whole file again before and after ffprobe (measurement.ts:62, :70). These are uncached full reads, separate from the identity-memoized hashMedia. A further gate commit follows.

The same coordinator already decided the opposite for artifact filing: "Measured after the gate is released, never inside it (Codex round 4) ... Held inside the world's serialisation envelope that blocks every other edit and every world switch" (filing.ts:495-503). fileGeneratedArtifact also hashes the whole buffer twice when expectedMediaHash is set (filing.ts:652-654).

Why it matters

While a video take arrives, every authored edit, every other take's arrival and every world switch waits behind two ffmpeg processes: seconds in normal use, up to 30 s at the timeouts. Scene passes and storyboard batches deliver many takes in sequence, so the editor feels frozen while generation finishes. Reading the file three times also adds I/O proportional to clip size.

Options
  1. ADo the media work before the gate, keep only the rename and records insideRecommended

    Run the hash, QC and poster on the landed file in the landing directory before entering the gate, drawing the poster into a staging path. Record the file's identity (dev, ino, size, mtime, ctime). Inside the gate, re-check that identity, rename the media and poster, and write take.json. The take still records QC from the exact bytes that arrived (#248, R-1 immutability).

  2. BQuick step: run QC and poster concurrently

    Promise.all the two ffmpeg runs inside the gate. About halves the time the gate is held, with no change to ordering semantics.

  3. CHash onceRecommended

    Pass the digest computed at arrival to measureProductionMedia and keep only the stat-identity checks around ffprobe, or memoize verifyProductionMedia on identity as scan.ts does. In fileGeneratedArtifact, compute the full digest once and slice it.

Impact

The gate is held for milliseconds instead of seconds (worst case 30 s+) per video take; the hold scales with clip length and the speed of the machine's ffmpeg. Full reads per arrival go from 3 to 1, saving about 200 MB of I/O and SHA-256 for a 100 MB clip. Not measured here, because ffmpeg was not run.

Risk

Take arrival is not replayable for most kinds (SPEC-013), so nothing new may throw: keep the best-effort handling in qc.ts and poster.ts. The poster must still appear together with the take. Tests: test/takes/takes.test.ts, qc.test.ts, poster.test.ts, test/media/measurement.test.ts and the replayable-finalization tests in test/queue. Check against SPEC-013 §2.2-§2.3 (R-1), SPEC-019 R-39 and issue #248.

Evidence

Plan → dispatch → poll → verify → land → ledger is not reimplemented per kind. Every loop enqueues into the one JobQueue; it is the dispatcher that submits, polls, verifies, lands and ledgers, and finalization reuses takes/arrival.ts or artifacts/filing.ts.

The loops differ where it matters. The audiobook run is one 690-line async function (audiobook-run.ts:841-1530) that awaits one job at a time and checkpoints the chapter record after each block. The frame run is a durable cursor file (productions/<id>/runs/<runId>.json), advanced on terminal events under serializeFileMutation (frame-run.ts:755-784). The comic Make card is 87 lines over injected ComicMakeOps.

The duplication is in the wiring. At least six modules each declare their own subset of enqueue, waitForJob, cancelJob, findJobs or jobs(match), actualCost and jobById, in different shapes: enqueue returns {jobIds, reason} in one and a bare id in another. coordinator.ts re-creates the lambdas at seven sites (2346, 11688, 11722, 15385, 17300, 18436, 24018). actualCost is a full ledger parse each time (PM-01), and jobById is listJobs().find(...) over the entire history (4572).

Why it matters

A generic pipeline abstraction would sit on top of a queue that already does the generic part, and it would have to accommodate three different durability models, so it would add code. What actually repeats is the port to the queue, and every copy is a place where a lookup is O(history) or a new run forgets cancellation.

Options
  1. AOne JobPort in queue/Recommended

    queue/job-port.ts defines one interface: enqueueOne(input, label), wait(id) (wrapping JobWaiters), cancel(id), get(id), find(predicate) and actualCost(id) (via the ledger index from PM-01). coordinator.ts builds it once. Audiobook, hear, drama, grouped-probe, generation-quotes and frame-run deps take a JobPort in place of their five ad hoc fields. Keep each loop's own orchestration.

  2. BGeneric generation pipeline (plan/dispatch/await/file/record stages)

    Not recommended. The shared stages already exist (JobQueue, takes/arrival.ts, artifacts/filing.ts), and the loops' durability rules are deliberately different: frame-run on-disk cursor, audiobook per-block checkpoint (SPEC-047 R-18), comic in-memory price ceiling. A framework would need options for all three.

  3. CLeave as is

    Acceptable, but every new run type copies the wiring again.

Impact

Roughly 60-100 lines of duplicated wiring and dependency declarations removed: 7 sites × about 6 lines in coordinator.ts, plus about 30 lines of interface fields in 6 modules. The cost lookup and job lookup fixes then land in one place, and the listJobs()-based lookups can move to get/find. Estimate from the counted sites.

Risk

JobWaiters' hold policy (coordinator.ts:6546) must keep holding audiobook and drama jobs that end before anyone waits. Tests: test/queue/job-waiters.test.ts, the audiobook, drama and hear tests, and test/productions/frame-run tests. Check against SPEC-047 R-16 and R-45.

Why it matters

The outbox protocol's complexity is justified by the crash model, but almost all of it sits in one file and one class, so every change to inputs, landing or recovery is reviewed against 3,000 lines. Evidence

pollToTerminal sleeps pollIntervalMs (default 1500) between polls, whatever the expected job length (dispatcher.ts:520, :1745). Every poll passes through captureProviderClient. It awaits a flushed start record before sending the request (capture.ts:337) and writes a flushed finish record afterwards, each via appendFlushed plus a stat (call-store.ts:106). The store rewrites itself once it holds more than 2,000 calls or 50 MB (:115). fal reads the result JSON when a job completes, and fetchArtifacts reads it again (fal.ts:455-458, 475-483). ComfyUI GETs /queue on every poll even though it also listens on a progress WebSocket (comfyui.ts:928-929).

Concurrency: a lane counts a job as in flight from submission through polling and landing (lane.inFlight at :864). Cloud providers default to 2 (baseConcurrency, :521) and local engines to 1 (coordinator.ts:4195).

Why it matters

For a 5-minute fal video: about 200 polls, about 400 fsyncs. For a 15-minute local H3 video: about 600 polls, about 1,200 fsyncs. Polls dominate the 2,000-call payload history and cause repeated compaction. Because the lane slot is held while the provider works remotely, a batch of 12 fal shots of about 3 minutes runs as 6 rounds (about 18 minutes) even when the account could run more at once.

Coordinator · CH · 14 findings

Conversations, assistant actions, the proposal gate and writing harnesses

The chat/action/gate core is deliberate and well guarded: per-run query leases, all-or-nothing turn validation, one acceptance gate and a crash-recoverable action lifecycle should all stay. The largest wins are in the plumbing around a turn rather than the model path: conversation reads and operational writes still go through ownedWrite, so one chat message triggers 4–5 full world rescans (the cost issue 1840 removed from world open), each turn re-discovers every conversation six times and re-validates the active log about 19 times, and log appends and the founding hand-off grow with log size (quadratically for the hand-off). On the prompt side, fixed instructions reach about 131k characters per production turn, the local-model 64k-token cap silently disappeared with the retired built-in harness, and no reply text is streamed. Simplification opportunities are a shared harness-turn helper (11 divergent loops), a declarative action definition (102 model kinds, each edited in 5–10 files) and converging the three ways a conversation point can land.

How this area is built, and how it was reviewed

A World Chat turn passes through five owners. The client sends world-chat-send; coordinator.ts guards it, dedupes the request id and builds a ConversationAuthoringService, which goes through ConversationInputs (per-conversation admission and the input queue) to sendNow. That validates the conversation and starts two things at once: the WorldChatRunner turn and, on a first message, a separate harness session that names the conversation.

The runner folds the append-only events.jsonl, resolves the model, pins the look, Bible and scene versions, renders the action guide from the arke-actions registry and assembles a budgeted prompt. It appends turn.started (fsync), mints a per-run lease, starts the loopback MCP world-query server, writes session files and opens a fresh native session (OpenCode v2, the Claude Agent SDK or the Codex app-server). While the model works it reads the world only through leased, paginated target reads that leave receipts.

The finished JSON answer is validated whole (evidence quotes, check plans, dry runs), corrected once if needed and appended as turn.completed with action intents; bindActions then prepares each card through its authority adapter, and a ready proposition's card stages a proposal. Acceptance is a separate human act: Approve on a card (lifecycle, then acceptDecided, then the gate and the world commit), Save on a rail point, or Wrap up into Approvals.

Around this core sit the founding conversation (a persistent session plus a blueprint), the founding build (a journalled four-wave driver), the Studio operational assistant, canon Q&A and local setup downloads. Durability and authority are handled carefully; most avoidable cost comes from the coordinator re-reading, rescanning and re-publishing state around each turn.

Scope and method

Read the turn path end to end: client frame sender, the coordinator handler, application/conversation-*, world-chat/run.ts and its dependencies, the three adapters, arke-actions/ (registry and lifecycle), gate/proposals.ts, the founding path (harness/genesis*.ts, world/founding-build.ts), setup/local-setup.ts, and studio-assistant/ and canon/ at outline level.

Counted with git grep and with read-only tsx scripts that import the source (action and guide counts, prompt sizes, positional-schema check). Benchmarked WorldChatStore read, append, discovery and the founding hand-off on synthetic logs, and ownedWrite against operationalWrite on a scratch copy of fixtures/worlds/the-undersong. All measurements ran in a Linux container without Defender and without the SQLite index, so they are floors, not Windows figures. Scripts are in the review folder's scripts/.

Not covered: running the app, the test suites or a real model; the client beyond its frame senders and button labels; the private specifications (SPEC-guarded items say "check against"). Earlier audits: AR-1 (application facade, 2026-08-04) is partly acted on through packages/coordinator/src/application/; AR-2 was resolved by the #828 decision to keep both adapter dependencies; ST-2 (synchronous OpenCode discovery) is acted on, discovery now uses async execFile; issue 1840 (2026-10-17) removed rescans from conversation discovery and recovery but not from conversation loads (CH-01).

CH-01Chat reads and operational writes still pay a full world rescan, 4–5 times per messagePerformanceUser journeyEffort SMedium riskHigh confidence

Evidence

WorldStore.ownedWrite always ends with await this.rescan(), and rescan runs scanWorld over every authored file, re-checks history snapshots, rewrites the scan state and syncs the index (store.ts:289-301, 860-878). Issue 1840 (commit b4934ed5f, 2026-10-17) moved conversation discovery and recovery to operationalWrite for exactly this reason, after measuring about 22 of a 30 s world open spent in four such scans on copies of two large worlds (~5.5 s per scan). The conversation paths left on ownedWrite only read, or write under the watcher-ignored .conversations and .history/*/prepared folders:

  • guardProductionSetupAuthority loads and folds the conversation under ownedWrite for every world-chat-* frame that names a conversation, before the handler runs (coordinator.ts:7721), including world-chat-send, world-chat-open and world-chat-send-status.
  • openWorldChat starts with await store.ownedWrite(() => service.load(conversationId)) (coordinator.ts:24703) and runs three times per ordinary send (once as soon as the send is handed to the runner, then twice through refreshConversationOutcome), four times when the namer renames. It broadcasts only after its rescan.
  • Every input-queue change runs two (input-journal.ts:215 and 222). Card preparation payloads (actions.ts:1881, called from six preparation paths), generation quotes (generation-quotes.ts:87, 125) and each cloud view_image disclosure (images.ts:161) run one each.

Measured on a scratch copy of fixtures/worlds/the-undersong (10-run average): ownedWrite(load) 66.4 ms, operationalWrite(load) 1.7 ms, bare load 1.0 ms.

Why it matters

Each rescan runs inside the world's single serialisation queue. It delays the guarded command itself, the moment the user's line and later the reply are published, and every other world write queued behind it (accepts, commits, input-queue changes). On worlds the size issue 1840 measured, one chat message costs about as many full scans as opening the world used to, and merely opening a conversation costs two.

Options
  1. AMove the operational call sites to the primitives issue 1840 introducedRecommended

    Use operationalWrite for the conversation loads and input-journal changes, and derivedWrite (ownership and serialisation, no rescan) for .history/*/prepared payloads and quotes. All three primitives keep verifyOwnership. operationalWrite re-discovers every conversation afterwards (store.ts:346-349), so prefer derivedWrite or ownedRead where no conversation row can change.

  2. BMake the setup guard a cheap lookupRecommended

    The guard only needs to know whether the conversation is an unfinished production setup. Answer that from the bundle's conversation rows or a small in-memory entry-context cache, and fall back to the full load only for setup conversations. Removes one rescan and one full fold from the front of every chat command.

  3. CSplit the checkpoint write out of WorldChatService.load

    load writes checkpoint.json as a side effect, which is why callers reached for ownedWrite. Make it a pure read and write the checkpoint in a background derivedWrite. Follow-up after A and B.

Impact

Removes 4–5 full world scans per chat message, 2 per conversation open, 2 per queued-input change and 1 per prepared card or cloud image view. Floor on the small fixture: ~65 ms per scan, ~0.26–0.33 s per message. On worlds the size issue 1840 measured, up to ~5.5 s per scan: tens of seconds of queued world work per message, one scan of it before the message is even admitted and one between the reply landing and being shown.

Risk

Anything that silently relied on the incidental rescan to refresh the bundle after an authored write outside the commit path would show stale data until the next scan, so audit adapters that write authored files without gateOp or commit. Ownership checks are kept (SPEC-002 §2.9, issue #827). Guarded by coordinator test/world/store.test.ts (the issue 1840 case), test/world-chat/*, test/productions/setup*.test.ts and the transport snapshot tests.

Evidence
  • ConversationInputs.start wraps each send's completion in observe, which calls changed, which is refreshConversationOutcome (conversation-inputs.ts:53 and 151, coordinator.ts:24511). The send handler then calls refreshConversationOutcome again after await inFlight (coordinator.ts:8703), and a third time if naming changed the title.
  • refreshConversations runs discoverConversations under operationalWrite, and operationalWrite runs discoverConversations again in refreshConversationRows (store.ts:333-349): two full discoveries per refresh, three refreshes per turn.
  • summariseOne reads and zod-validates each conversation's entire events.jsonl before looking at the checkpoint (discover.ts:51-62). The checkpoint saves only the fold, only when exactly current, and is written every 100 events (checkpoint.ts:102-108).
  • Counted along the code path, the active log is read and validated about 19 times per ordinary turn (dispatch guard 1, queue reads 3, sendNow 2, runner 2, appends 2, discoveries 6, loads 3) and every other conversation 6 times. Each new WorldChatStore also re-reads the file once for its per-instance torn-tail check (store.ts:143-147, 203-212).
  • For a conversation with attachments, every load synchronously reads and parses every Bench session in the world, twice, to compute a delete-button reason (service.ts:70-80, bench/chat-reads.ts:97-108).

Measured: discoverConversations 120 ms for 30 conversations of 60 turns (9 MB); store.read 7.7 ms at 100 turns and 17.3 ms at 300.

Why it matters

Parsing and validation are synchronous CPU on the coordinator's event loop, so they stall every client's WebSocket while they run, and the reply is published only after these refreshes. The cost grows with the total size of every conversation in the world, not with the conversation in use.

Options
  1. ADelete the duplicate refresh and reuse the discoveryRecommended

    Drop the handler's post-completion refreshConversationOutcome (observe already ran it) and let refreshConversations hand its discovered rows to the store instead of operationalWrite discovering again.

  2. BCache validated events and summary rows by file identityRecommended

    Keep a per-conversation cache keyed by (size, mtimeMs) or by the in-process writer's tail; on growth parse only the appended bytes. Discovery then costs a stat per unchanged conversation. The append-time tail check still guards foreign edits.

  3. CFold incrementally from the checkpoint

    Apply only events after throughSeq to the checkpoint view instead of refolding the whole log whenever the checkpoint is behind.

  4. DCompute the Bench deletion reason lazilyRecommended

    Only when the person opens the delete control (blockedFromDeletion already exists), or cache it by the .sessions folder's identity.

Impact

A alone: 6 to 2 discoveries per turn (about −480 ms in the 30-conversation synthetic world on Linux) and one fewer snapshot broadcast. A with B: discovery proportional to conversations that changed, and active-log validation from about 19 passes to about 3.

Risk

A and D are behaviour-preserving. B needs care so a cache never masks a foreign edit (keep the append-time digest check). Covered by coordinator test/transport.test.ts (snapshot sequencing), test/world-chat discovery and recovery tests and the issue 1840 store test.

Where

  • packages/contracts/src/events.ts:2274-2293
  • packages/coordinator/src/world-chat/run.ts:1167-1171
  • packages/coordinator/src/world-chat/run.ts:1347-1375

Evidence
  • askOnce turns message.delta into one progress label per stretch of writing and keeps only message.completed (run.ts:306-331). The only event during a turn is world-chat.progress with a label (events.ts:2289). The founding chat behaves the same (genesis.ts:376-385).
  • After the answer: whole-result validation, a sequential check plan per candidate (run.ts:1167-1171), dry runs, and up to two corrective asks (run.ts:899-957).
  • turn.completed is appended, then bindActions prepares every card one after another (conversation-runs.ts:237-243); a ready candidate's card stages a proposal through savePoint (actions.ts:5816-5837). Only then does the turn resolve and the coordinator refresh and publish (CH-01, CH-02).
  • The answer format puts the reply first: {"reply": "...", "candidateOperations": [...]} (roster.ts:372).
Why it matters

People wait through the whole model turn with a single verb on screen, often tens of seconds to minutes, and then through card preparation and refreshes after the reply already exists on disk. This is the biggest lever on how fast the assistant feels.

Options
  1. APublish the reply before preparing cardsRecommended

    Refresh the conversation as soon as turn.completed is durable; cards show as preparing (the fold already carries actionPrepareIntents) and update when bound.

  2. BStream a provisional replyRecommended

    Decode the reply string incrementally from deltas (it is the first field) and emit a transient world-chat.reply-delta; the client shows it as provisional until the validated turn lands and replaces it on rejection. Never persisted.

  3. CRun per-candidate check plans in parallel and show elapsed timeRecommended

    The check plans are independent coordinator-local reads; Promise.all over candidates. An elapsed timer beside the progress verb sets expectations without naming entities.

Impact

A removes card preparation (proposal staging per ready candidate) and one refresh from reply latency. B moves time to first words from the end of the turn to the first tokens, typically a few seconds. Not measured; depends on model and world.

Risk

Issue #70 §8.3's all-or-nothing rule: a streamed reply can still be rejected, so it must be marked provisional and never written to the log. Progress text must still not name entities (the R-18 rule cited in contracts events.ts). Tests: coordinator test/world-chat/run*.test.ts and the client chat tests.

Evidence

Measured by importing the modules:

  • world-builder system prompt 34,921 characters (brief 5,047 plus a 28,108-character result-shape postscript);
  • action guide: world 29,297 full or 9,101 compact; production 95,724 full or 35,994 compact. Compact still carries about 14k of always-on prose (the effects guide alone is 6,566) plus one line per kind (21,668 for 102 production kinds).
  • The full guide is used whenever it fits a fifth of the budget (action-guide.ts:244). With a 200k-token window budgetFor gives about 595k characters, so production threads send the 96k guide every turn.
  • The Bible (up to 200,000 characters) and every tombstone are never trimmed (context.ts:512-519).
  • Each turn opens a fresh harness session and resends everything (run.ts:840-851), and the per-turn entry and subject line sits before the guide (run.ts:1510-1515), so prefix caches can reuse at most the system prompt.
Why it matters

Every turn pays for these tokens in money on cloud models and in prefill time on local ones. The code's own figure: a 12B model reads 121,000 tokens in about three minutes on a 10 GB card, roughly 670 tokens a second (context.ts:107-113).

Options
  1. AScope the guide to the threadRecommended

    Full entries only for kinds the entry context prioritises (the priorities table exists), names only for the rest, and describe_action on demand (already served).

  2. BOrder the prompt static-firstRecommended

    Put the guide and other stable sections before the per-turn entry and subject narration, or into the session's system prompt, so provider and Ollama prefix caches can reuse them across the per-turn sessions.

  3. CTrim duplicated prose and bound tombstones

Coordinator + desktop · RP · 14 findings

Runtime performance: persistence, world loading, snapshot/transport and desktop startup

The runtime cost is dominated by re-reading, not by flushing: every authored write rescans the whole world (records, change log and every conversation log), and the app-global journals are re-read and schema-parsed in full per completed job, per world change, per reconnect and three times at start-up. Measured on Linux, one no-file commit on a 4,000-artifact world costs ~0.9 s and ~6,200 file reads, a 5,000-job history turns a 0.23 s Node start-up into 3.2 s and costs ~0.8 s per completed job, and ProviderCallStore rewrites its whole file on every provider call once it holds 2,000 calls. All of it runs on Electron's main thread. The 2026-08-04 startup audit is resolved (window first, async discovery, single-pass queue recovery, registry discovery), but optional probes and history reads still sit serially before ready. The deliberate invariants (flush order, ownership checks, transport authentication) are cheap and can stay; the wins come from incremental reads, identity caches and deleting dead rebuilds.
