How this area is built, and how it was reviewed

Electron main hosts the coordinator. After app.whenReady the desktop reads the theme, creates and paints the launch window, then StartupController runs initialize(): FsWorldProvider.ensureAppRoot (including an app-index rebuild from the job and ledger logs), the child-ledger sweep, harness discovery, provider and engine construction, createStudioHost, and StudioServer.start, which runs Coordinator.startApplication (job and ledger seeds, recovery services, provider and tool probes, queue recovery, world listing, founding-build peeks). Remote access and a spool sweep follow, then ready reaches the renderer over private IPC.

Opening a world takes the lock, recovers interrupted commits, and runs scanWorld, which reads every record file sixteen at a time, hashes and schema-parses it, reads the change log and every conversation log, checks history snapshots, writes the scan state, opens or rebuilds the SQLite world index by fingerprint, and starts a recursive watcher. Every later commit, owned write or gate operation ends with the same full rescan.

Operational journals (jobs, ledger, provider calls) append through appendFlushed behind a per-file WriteQueue and are read back whole; the change log is unflushed and rolls at 16 MB. The read model folds validated events; Transport validates every outgoing frame, pages artifacts, jobs and ledger per connection in 1 MB pages, sends the rest of the state as a barrier snapshot, coalesces refreshes at 250 ms and bounds delivery through SocketWriter (32 MB, 256 frames, waiting snapshots superseded). Every hello gets a fresh full snapshot. The remote gateway forwards frames verbatim with backpressure.

Scope and method

Examined: coordinator world/ (store, scan, commit, provider, watcher, lock, atomic), index-db/, storage/ inventory and monitor, recovery/ timers, read-model.ts, snapshot-pages.ts, socket-writer.ts, transport.ts, change-log.ts, ndjson.ts, flushed-append.ts, journal-record.ts, child-ledger.ts, system-resources.ts, diagnostics-snapshot.ts, supervisor.ts health timers, the queue journal/ledger/call-store persistence, the snapshot and startup parts of coordinator.ts, remote-access gateway forwarding, and apps/desktop main.ts, startup.ts, preload.ts, updates.ts, remote-access.ts, performance-spool.ts, system-resources.ts.

Method: code reading with git grep counts; nine micro-benchmarks that import the real coordinator and contracts source through the repository's tsx (scripts and outputs in the review folder: bench-append.mjs, bench-callstore.mts, bench-journals.mts, bench-world.mts, bench-bundle-hash.mts, bench-changelog.mts, bench-conversations.mts, bench-spend.mts, bench-startup.mts); two CPU profiles (one commit loop, one 5,000-job start-up); fs/promises call counting for one scan and one commit. Synthetic data is shaped from the committed fixtures (fixtures/queue/jobs.jsonl, fixtures/ledger.jsonl, fixtures/worlds/the-undersong) inflated to large-world sizes; journal rows ~1.45 KB, 6 rows per job.

All numbers are from a Linux container (4 vCPU Xeon 2.3 GHz, ext4 on virtio, Node 22.23) and are not Windows numbers: no Defender scan-on-open, no NTFS, no where.exe. Not covered: client store application cost (client reviewer), Electron-level frame timing, real users' record sizes and job counts, provider pipeline internals beyond the call store, and the private specifications (SPEC citations are by id only).

Evidence

commitUnserialised ends with rescan([...paths, "world.json"]) (store.ts:442), and rescan (store.ts:860) is a full scanWorld, then checkCurrentHistorySnapshots (re-reads every versioned record and its history snapshot and hashes both), then saveScanState (rewrites the whole pretty-printed manifest with fsync), then an index update. ownedWrite (store.ts:289) does the same after every app-owned write, including every job landing (landInWorld, coordinator.ts:3979) and every saved audiobook block (docs/filesystem-operations.md:301).

gateOp rescans again in its finally unless the caller passes { finalWrite: "commit" } (store.ts:278). git grep counts: 131 gateOp call sites, 2 opt-ins (both in artifacts/filing.ts), 67 commitUnserialised calls. Example: createEpisode (productions/ops.ts:747) is gateOp + commitUnserialised, so two full scans.

A scan also reads the world's whole changes.jsonl (scan.ts:1362, append-only, never rewritten) and every conversation's whole events.jsonl with a zod parse per event (discover.ts:56 reads the log before it looks at the checkpoint). applyCommit rebuilds the whole SQLite index for any artifacts/ or references/ path (world-index.ts:200) and always recomputes bundleFingerprint, a JSON.stringify of nearly the whole bundle.

Measured (Linux container, synthetic world = fixture + 4,000 artifact sidecars with 2.7 KB prompts + 1,000 takes):

  • scanWorld 556 ms; first open 899 ms; reopen 757 ms; reload 471 ms.
  • One no-file commit (renameWorld) 918 ms median of 5; fs/promises calls for that one commit: 6,223 readFile, 1,078 stat, 46 readdir.
  • bundleFingerprint 57-68 ms; full WorldIndex.rebuild 116 ms; an artifact-path applyCommit 140 ms.
  • discoverConversations with 20 conversations x 500 events (20 MB) 552 ms per scan; reading and parsing one 1 MB log 22 ms.

The code already records the field cost: "On a large world each rescan cost seconds" (store.ts:327, issue 1840) and "3,898 artifact sidecars took 2.6 s in turn and 0.71 s sixteen at once" (scan.ts:433).

Why it matters

A single keystroke-level save, a take landing or an accepted proposal costs O(world size + world history) of file opens, hashing and schema parsing on the coordinator's only thread, which is Electron's main thread. During a picture run every landed picture triggers this, which matches the 2026-10-24 incidents recorded in socket-writer.ts and coalesced-reads.ts. On Windows every one of the ~6,000 opens per scan is also scanned by Defender, which is why the comments speak of seconds.

Options
  1. AIdentity-keyed scan cache with structural sharingRecommended

    Cache, per record path, {size, mtimeMs, ctimeMs} -> {sha256, parsed value or problem} across scans of an open store, as hashMedia already does for media (scan.ts:358). A rescan still lists every directory and stats every file, so additions, deletions and outside edits are still discovered, but unchanged files skip read, sha256, JSON.parse and zod. Re-read any file whose mtime falls within ~2 s of the previous scan start (git's racy-clean rule) so coarse-timestamp volumes (FAT/exFAT) cannot hide a same-size rewrite. Returning the previous parsed object when the hash is unchanged also makes rows reference-stable for SnapshotPages, the client store and the index (see RP-07). Expected: ~6,200 reads per commit become ~1,100 stats plus the changed files.

  2. BFirst step: opt the remaining gate operations into finalWrite: commit

    The mechanism exists and is documented (store.ts:270-278, filesystem-operations.md:301). Audit the ~65 gateOp bodies whose last filesystem write is commitUnserialised and pass the option. Halves the scans for those operations with no new machinery. Each opt-in needs the existing reconciliation test for its operation.

  3. CMake the post-commit checks incremental

    Derive the WorldIndex fingerprint from the scan manifest hashes (already computed per file) plus the index schema version instead of stringifying the bundle (~60 ms per commit and per open). After a commit, run checkCurrentHistorySnapshots only for the changed paths and reuse scan.manifest[path] instead of re-reading the live file. Index artifact/reference commits by row instead of a full rebuild. Check against SPEC-003 R-3 (fingerprint as staleness signal).

  4. DTail-read append-only logs inside the scan

    Keep a byte offset and parsed prefix for changes.jsonl, and use a conversation's checkpoint throughSeq plus a tail read to get tailSeq instead of reading the whole log. Same helper as RP-02 option A.

  5. EPatch the bundle per changed path

    Largest win (no walk at all after an in-app commit) but scanWorld derives cross-file state (problems, references, candidates, measurements) in one pass; splitting it is L effort with high regression risk. Not recommended before A-D.

Impact

On the synthetic large world: commit ~0.9 s -> est. 0.15-0.25 s with A+B+C (stat walk ~1,100 entries + changed files + index delta); estimated from the profile split (scan 50-60%, fingerprint ~10%, index ~10-15%, double scans). Chat-heavy worlds gain more (552 ms of conversation parsing per scan at 20 MB of logs). On Windows the saving per avoided open is larger than on Linux.

Risk

Outside-edit detection and reconciliation depend on the manifest (SPEC-002 R-23, R-28) and history checks (issue 979). An identity cache must fail toward re-reading. Guarded by coordinator test/world/*.test.ts (watcher, reconcile, history), test/world-provider.test.ts and the gate tests; the B opt-ins are guarded by each operation's tests.

RP-02App-global journals are re-read and zod-parsed in full per completed job, per world change and three times at start-upPerformanceEffort MMedium riskHigh confidence
Where

  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:4826
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:4963
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:24936
  • packages/coordinator/src/spend/read.ts:21
  • packages/coordinator/src/spend/ledger.ts:107
  • packages/coordinator/src/queue/journal.ts:67
  • packages/coordinator/src/queue/dispatcher.ts:2105
  • packages/coordinator/src/queue/dispatcher.ts:2320
Evidence

jobs.jsonl and ledger.jsonl are append-only and never compacted (journal.ts header, ledger.ts:12). Readers re-parse them whole:

  • Each terminal job: appendLedgerOnce calls ledger.has(jobId) (dispatcher.ts:2105), wired to a strict full read plus .some() (coordinator.ts:3954). 13 other sites do (await this.ledger.readAll()).find(e => e.jobId === id) for one job (coordinator.ts:2351, 4574, 6594-6825, 11695, 15393, 20802, 23678), and two more read the whole ledger for free-credit totals (1788, 1797).
  • Each terminal job.updated, every ledger.appended, every bench.* event and every setDisplayWorld schedules readProductionSpend (coordinator.ts:4963, 4826), which parses the whole ledger, every journal row with JobSchema.parse, and every Bench session log of the world (spend/read.ts:21). It is coalesced, so during a run it re-runs back to back.
  • Start-up parses the journal three times (AppIndex rebuild, seed(), jobQueue.start()) and the ledger three or four times.

Measured with the real readers (Linux, 6 journal rows of ~1.45 KB per job):

  • 5,000 jobs (43.5 MB journal, 1.3 MB ledger): ledger strict read 23 ms, readHistory 853 ms, seed readNdjson 676 ms, readProductionSpend 816 ms.
  • 20,000 jobs (174 MB): ledger 101 ms, readHistory 2,688 ms, seed 2,530 ms.
  • Node host time-to-ready (no harness, no probes): 233 ms empty, 858 ms at 1,000 jobs, 3,163 ms at 5,000 jobs; CPU profile: 1.36 s GC, 0.53 s zod _parse.

The same whole-log pattern also exists in WorldChatStore.append (inspectTail reads, parses and hashes the whole conversation log per append, world-chat/store.ts:246) - owned by the chat reviewer.

Why it matters

Cost grows with lifetime use, not with the work being done: a heavy user (the comments cite a world with 3,898 artifacts, so thousands of jobs) pays most of a second of blocked main thread per completed job and seconds at every launch, and it gets worse every week.

Options
  1. AShared incremental NDJSON tail reader with an in-memory indexRecommended

    One helper that keeps {dev, ino, size, byteOffset, parsedRows} per file. On read it stats the file; if identity matches and the size grew it parses only the appended bytes up to the last newline, otherwise (repair, rename, shrink, other inode) it re-reads fully. LedgerFile keeps a Map<jobId, LedgerEntry> for has/lookup; readProductionSpend, seed and queue start consume the cached rows. Semantics stay intact: a failed stat/read still throws in the strict path and degrades with unavailable in the tolerant one, and a rejected or uncertain append invalidates the cache so presence is re-read from disk, never inferred (CLAUDE.md journal rule, SPEC-009 R-16).

  2. BFeed production spend from the event stream

    Keep production-spend evidence in memory from job.updated/ledger.appended and read files only at world open. Smaller change in spend/read.ts but duplicates fold logic that already exists in the dispatcher.

  3. CCompact jobs.jsonl

    Folding the journal to latest rows conflicts with production spend's need for the complete history including tombstones (docs/development/production-spend.md) and with the append-only crash model; not recommended.

Impact

At 5,000 jobs: ~0.85 s of main-thread parsing per completed job becomes a few ms (one stat + appended bytes); start-up loses ~1.5 s of the 3.2 s (together with RP-04, ~2.9 s). Estimated from the per-reader timings above.

Risk

Ledger dedupe must never append on unknown presence (SPEC-009 R-16, ledger.ts:96-106) and the spend view must keep its unavailable flag (SPEC-032 R-21). The standalone server and desktop must not share an app root concurrently (single-instance lock assumed). Guarded by test/spend/*.test.ts, test/queue/dispatcher.test.ts, ledger and journal tests.

RP-03ProviderCallStore rewrites its whole file on every provider call once 2,000 calls are retained (and spawns icacls.exe each time on Windows)PerformanceEffort SLow riskHigh confidence
Where
  • packages/coordinator/src/providers/call-store.ts:174
  • packages/coordinator/src/providers/call-store.ts:177
  • packages/coordinator/src/providers/call-store.ts:187
  • packages/providers/src/capture.ts:337
  • packages/providers/src/capture.ts:509
Evidence

After every write: if (this.current.size > MAX_CALLS || size > MAX_FILE_BYTES) await this.compact(); (call-store.ts:174). compact keeps exactly the newest MAX_CALLS = 2,000 records by count (177-191), so the next start() makes 2,001 and compacts again. Compaction is an atomicWriteFile (write, fsync, rename) followed by lockDown, which on Windows runs icacls.exe (call-store.ts:26-38).

Every captured HTTP request, including each status poll (capture.ts:509), records start, respond and finish (three flushed appends), and the request waits for start (capture.ts:337).

Measured with the real class (Linux): start+respond+finish per call 1.5-4.5 ms below 2,000 retained calls, 29-31 ms above; the file stays at 2,002 lines and 4.1 MB is rewritten per call. Because compaction keeps by count only, a retained set larger than 50 MB would compact on every write (three per call) - code-read, not observed.

Why it matters

A video job is polled tens of times, so an active user crosses 2,000 calls within a few dozen jobs and from then on every poll pays a multi-MB rewrite plus a process spawn before its request is sent.

Options
  1. AHysteresis plus a byte budget, ACL onceRecommended

    Compact only when retained calls exceed ~1.25 x MAX_CALLS (or the file exceeds ~2 x its live size), down to MAX_CALLS and to at most half of MAX_FILE_BYTES. Keep atomicWriteFile (the compaction still syncs, as the invariant requires). Apply the restrictive ACL to the provider-calls directory once so new files inherit it, or only when the file is created, instead of after every compaction. Update the wording in filesystem-operations.md:38.

  2. BFewer flushed appends per poll

    Fold respond into finish for non-submit operations. Keeps the flushed start before the external request. Check against SPEC-009 §2.2.1 before changing what is durable when.

  3. CRecord polls only on change or failure

    A product decision about payload history in Activity; cuts appends by an order of magnitude.

Impact

Compactions drop from one per call to one per ~500 calls; per-poll overhead returns to ~2 ms on Linux and loses an icacls process spawn on Windows (spawn typically 50-150 ms there; not measured here).

Risk

Retention bound becomes approximate (up to ~2,500 records). Flush order is unchanged. Guarded by coordinator provider call-store tests.

Where
  • packages/coordinator/src/index-db/app-index.ts:226
  • packages/coordinator/src/index-db/app-index.ts:237
  • packages/coordinator/src/index-db/app-index.ts:263
  • packages/coordinator/src/index-db/app-index.ts:286

Evidence

FsWorldProvider.ensureAppRoot calls appIndex.rebuildFromLogs(jobs.jsonl, ledger.jsonl) on first use (provider.ts:145), the first awaited step of desktop initialize() (main.ts:751). It deletes both tables and re-inserts every journal row (one upsertJob per transition row) and every ledger entry.

The file's own comment says nothing in production reads these tables (app-index.ts:226-236). git grep confirms: no callers of spendByProvider, spendByWeek, upsertJob or appendLedger outside rebuildFromLogs and tests.

upsertJob/appendLedger/upsertWorld/getMeta call this.db.prepare(...) per row. Measured: rebuild 239 ms at 1,000 jobs, 1,414 ms at 5,000, 4,512 ms at 20,000 (Linux); in the 5,000-job start-up profile better-sqlite3 prepare alone took 372 ms self time.

Why it matters

Pure dead work on the critical path to ready that grows with history.

Options
  1. AStop rebuilding until a consumer existsRecommended

    Drop the jobs/ledger mirror (or rebuild lazily on the first spendBy* call). The world registry part of the app index stays. Check against SPEC-003 R-5, which describes jobs and ledger mirrored into app.db.

  2. BKeep it, but off the critical path and cheaper

    Run after ready in the background, hoist the prepared statements out of the loops (better-sqlite3 statements are reusable), and set synchronous = NORMAL for this rebuildable cache.

Impact

-0.24 s to -4.5 s of start-up depending on history (measured); removes ~35,000 statement compilations at 5,000 jobs.

Risk

Only tests read the tables. Spec wording (SPEC-003 R-5) may need an amendment. Guarded by test/index-db app-index tests.

RP-05The coordinator shares Electron's main thread, so its long synchronous passes stall the window, IPC and every renderer requestPerformanceUser journeyEffort MMedium riskMedium confidence
Where
  • apps/desktop/src/main.ts:664
  • apps/desktop/src/main.ts:139
  • packages/coordinator/src/coalesced-reads.ts:22
  • packages/coordinator/src/world/scan.ts:351
  • packages/coordinator/src/socket-writer.ts:34
Evidence

The coordinator is embedded in Electron main (main.ts:139-142, SPEC-001 D2). Every renderer request passes session.webRequest.onBeforeSendHeaders for <all_urls> (main.ts:664), which is serviced on that thread.

Synchronous blocks measured in this review (Linux): journal parse loops 0.68-2.7 s (RP-02), scan parse/hash per commit (RP-01), canonical bundle hash 155-206 ms (RP-09), whole-snapshot zod parse 297 ms for 20 MB (RP-07). The code records field incidents: audiobookListening is "about five seconds of the coordinator's one thread" (coalesced-reads.ts:22-30, 2026-10-24); sockets closed "about ten times in ten minutes" during a picture run (socket-writer.ts:30-38); scan.ts:351 "stalling the Electron main process".

Why it matters

While the coordinator parses, the window cannot be dragged or resized smoothly, theme/IPC messages wait, and media requests wait for the header hook - the user sees a frozen app rather than a slow operation.

Options
  1. ARemove the big synchronous passes and add yield pointsRecommended

    Fix RP-01/02/06/09 first; in the remaining long loops (NDJSON readers, conversation reads, production-spend derivation) yield with await setImmediate() every few hundred rows or ~20 ms, as story-export.ts and storage/inventory.ts already do.

  2. BRun the coordinator in an Electron utilityProcess

    The renderer already talks to it over loopback WebSocket and HTTP, so the renderer path is unchanged; main keeps window, dialogs and IPC and forwards the few host callbacks (dialogs, shell, safeStorage). L effort; the capability must still be minted in main and passed privately (CLAUDE.md transport rules). Check against SPEC-001 D2.

  3. Cworker_threads for pure derivations

    Production spend, fingerprints and canonical hashes are pure functions of data; moving them to a worker costs a structured clone of the input.

Impact

Removes multi-hundred-millisecond to multi-second UI stalls during runs and start-up; B isolates the window entirely. The UI effect is inferred from the measured blocking times, not measured in Electron.

Risk

Option B changes process topology: shutdown drain (Coordinator.stop() via shutdownConfirmed), child ledger ownership and transport-auth handoff must be re-proven (desktop test/transport-auth.test.ts, preload-auth.test.ts, smoke:main).

Shared · CT · 15 findings

Shared contracts, the engine package, cross-package duplication and dependencies

The contracts package is a well-factored vocabulary (one schema per wire or disk shape, pure calculations, no module-load side effects), but it is consumed as one eager barrel: any import evaluates all 251 modules, about 36,700 zod v3 schema instances and three.js, which costs 190–220 ms and about 57 MB of heap per process when bundled and 470–550 ms per test process under tsx. The cheapest large levers are a sideEffects: false flag (measured: engine core bundle −81%), removing zod v3's per-instance method binding (measured: −30% evaluation time, −50% heap) and not re-validating frames that are already validated (each event is zod-parsed at emit, again per connection, and again in the client). Logic that must agree across the wire is written more than once: 15 canonical-JSON functions with at least three different semantics, and a ClientState event fold duplicated arm for arm in the coordinator read model and the client store. Truly dead code is small (about 720 lines), but 42% of the barrel's runtime exports are imported by no other package, three declared events are never emitted, schema-invalid commands are dropped without any reply to the screen that sent them, and a zod v4 migration would make startup worse, not better (measured 4–6× slower schema construction and 4–5× the heap).

How this area is built, and how it was reviewed

@arke-studio/contracts is a private, source-only workspace package: main and types both point at ./src/index.ts, with no exports map and no sideEffects field. It holds zod v3 schemas for every wire and disk shape (1,331 exported schemas; ClientMessageSchema is one discriminated union of 556 command kinds and DomainEventSchema one of 248 event types), their inferred types, and a large body of pure domain calculations. Its runtime dependencies are zod (^3.23.8, resolved 3.25.76) and three (^0.185.1), the latter only for camera paths and projection in staging.ts and stage-camera.ts. Three plain-JavaScript modules (interactive-player.js, audiobook-player.js, story-state.js) have hand-written .d.ts files, and the two players also have generated string copies that the exporters inline.

Everything is consumed through one barrel (index.ts: 237 export * lines and 5 named re-exports) from 1,818 import statements; none uses a subpath. No module has top-level statements other than declarations, so loading has no side effect beyond constructing values. The internal graph is uneven: 139 modules reach fewer than 10 others, while frames.ts, client-state.ts and events.ts each reach 169–178 of the 251.

Use is lopsided. Of the public runtime code, 21,218 lines (932 values in 62 modules) are used only by the coordinator, 4,525 lines only by the client and 7,638 lines by both. At runtime the coordinator reaches 92% of contracts' value code, the client 61%, and the client would reach 37% if it did not validate incoming frames itself.

@arke-studio/engine is a 21-line facade that esbuild-bundles coordinator application/* services with contracts for external Node hosts. @arke-studio/confined-tools (781 lines) holds the Codex harness's pinned-root file tools and has one consumer.

Scope and method

Examined packages/contracts (all 251 runtime modules, the index.ts barrel, its package.json and tests), packages/engine, packages/confined-tools, the contracts boundary with coordinator, client, desktop, adapters, providers and voice, and every workspace package.json against package-lock.json.

Method, with scripts kept in the review folder:

  • TypeScript checker over the barrel to list all 4,636 exports and resolve each to its declaration (exports-census.mjs); parsing of every tracked file outside contracts for names imported or re-exported from @arke-studio/contracts.
  • A reference-graph reachability pass over 5,596 top-level declarations, once with all edges and once with value-position edges only (reach.mjs, reach-rt.mjs).
  • esbuild rebuilds of the contracts barrel, the desktop main bundle (same options as apps/desktop/scripts/build.mjs), the engine's two entries and an approximation of the client bundle, plus a Rollup tree-shaking experiment over the client's 834 runtime imports (bundle-*.mjs, rollup-treeshake*.mjs). All output went to the scratch folder.
  • Timed imports in fresh Node 22.23 processes (plain and through tsx), a CPU profile, a zod construction census (zod-census.mjs), zod v3 versus v4 and v4-mini micro-benchmarks (zod-v3-v4.mjs, zod-4.4.mjs), an experiment with a no-bind copy of zod 3.25.76, frame-validation costs (parse-cost.ts) and a synthetic change-log replay (changelog-cost.ts).
  • Vocabulary checks of every event type and command kind against coordinator, client and desktop source (vocab-usage.mjs, event-handling.mjs, event-emission.mjs), a dependency-to-import map (dep-usage.mjs) and a cross-package duplicate-name scan (dup-names.mjs), each lead read by hand.

Earlier audit: the 2026-08-04 architecture-reuse report's AR-1 (a public command facade) has been partly acted on through coordinator application/* services and the engine package (engine.md, epic #1182); AR-2 was resolved by decision in #828 and is not re-raised; AR-3 (no compiled artifact) was acted on for external hosts by the engine's bundled build. Its "DRY: clean" verdict no longer holds at the contracts boundary (CT-05, CT-06, CT-14).

Not covered: the real Vite production build (approximated), snapshot sizes of a large real world, browser or phone timings (Node/V8 in this container is the proxy), the full test suite (not run), and the private specs (absent; SPEC citations are quoted only as places to check). Timings come from one Linux container and are indicative. Process note: one early esbuild run wrote a bundle to /home/user/ArkeStudio/out/ through a relative output path; I moved it to the scratch folder at once and git status was clean afterwards.

Findings

CT-01Any import evaluates the whole contracts package: 251 modules, ~36,700 zod schemas and three.jsPerformanceSimplificationEffort SLow riskHigh confidence
Where
  • packages/contracts/package.json:8-16
  • packages/contracts/src/index.ts:1-260
  • packages/contracts/src/stage-camera.ts:2
  • packages/contracts/src/staging.ts:1
  • packages/client/vite.config.ts:13-25
  • packages/engine/scripts/build.mjs:7-9
  • apps/desktop/scripts/build.mjs:13-23
Evidence

index.ts re-exports 237 modules with export *; all 1,818 import statements use the bare specifier, and the package has no exports map or sideEffects field. An esbuild bundle of the barrel has 251 inputs, so importing one constant loads everything, including three.

Measured in fresh Node 22.23 processes:

  • Bundled barrel (zod and three external): 190–220 ms, heap +57 MB. Through tsx, as every test and the dev coordinator load it: 470–550 ms warm, 1,314 ms with a cold tsx cache. Single modules through tsx: money.ts 2.5 ms, ids.ts 25–36 ms, timeline.ts 138–152 ms, frames.ts 334–446 ms.
  • Zod census during evaluation: 36,723 instances (8,153 ZodObject, 7,718 ZodString, 4,482 ZodNumber, 4,171 ZodNever, 3,321 ZodOptional...), of which 24,088 are reachable from the 1,331 exported schemas; the rest are intermediates of chained calls.
  • CPU profile of the bundled import: about 111 ms compiling source, 73 ms in zod constructors, 62 ms garbage collection, 35 ms module top level.
  • Where the bytes land: 3,103 KB (17.8%) of the 17.4 MB unminified desktop main.cjs; 1,413 of the engine core's 1,488 KB; 1,282 KB of the client's 6,374 KB minified JS.

The package qualifies for "sideEffects": false: a TypeScript pass found zero top-level statements other than declarations, no top-level let, no side-effect-only imports and no top-level mutation. Measured effect of the flag: engine core 1,488 → 279 KB; client −6 KB on its own; with Rollup treeshake.manualPureFunctions: ["z", "valueSchema"] the client's contracts slice goes 1,260 → 1,166 KB minified, its evaluation 164–178 → 141–150 ms and heap 53 → 47 MB.

Who needs how much (value-position reachability): coordinator 92% of contracts' value code, client 61%; providers need 73 of 251 modules, voice 14, the three adapters about 127.

Why it matters

Every process pays this before it does anything useful: the desktop main process and the renderer (each), every phone page load through remote access, every external engine host, and each test file that touches contracts (at least 949 of 1,188 test files import it directly, and node --test runs one process per file). At roughly 0.5 s per tsx test process that is on the order of 8–9 CPU-minutes per full test run per platform (estimate: about 1,000 barrel-loading processes × the measured warm import). Because nothing is tree-shakeable today, server-only code and validation-only schemas also ship to, and are evaluated by, every browser.

Options
  1. AAdd "sideEffects": false to contracts and mark zod calls pure in the client's Vite configRecommended

    One line in packages/contracts/package.json plus build.rollupOptions.treeshake.manualPureFunctions: ["z", "valueSchema"] in packages/client/vite.config.ts. Keeps the barrel and every import site. Measured: engine core −1.2 MB, client −94 KB minified and about 25 ms less startup evaluation. It is also the precondition for the larger client saving in CT-03. Does nothing for the coordinator, which needs almost all of it.

  2. BLet tests and small consumers import single modules

    Point the 112 contracts tests that import ../src/index.js at the module under test, and add an exports map with a ./* subpath so voice, providers and confined-tools import only what they use (14, 73 and 1 modules instead of 251). Saves about 0.4 s per such test process (roughly 75–185 files, 30–75 CPU-seconds per run). Costs an import-style rule and some churn; coordinator and client tests still load nearly everything through their own src.

  3. CSplit the barrel into subpath entries (schemas, geometry, players)

    Large churn across 1,818 import statements for a small product gain, because the coordinator reaches 92% of the code anyway and the client 61%. Not recommended now.

Impact

Option A, measured on scratch rebuilds: engine core bundle 1,488 → 279 KB; client contracts slice 1,260 → 1,166 KB minified, about 25 ms and 6 MB less at page load on this container's CPU. Vite's own numbers may differ by a few percent from the Rollup experiment.

Risk

With sideEffects: false a bundler may drop a module none of whose exports are used; contracts has no load-time effects (checked statement by statement), so nothing observable is lost. Vite dev ignores the flag. manualPureFunctions assumes schema construction is pure, which it is. Verify with npm run build, the engine pack test (packages/engine/test/pack.test.mjs) and the client smoke checks.

CT-02Zod v3 binds 24 methods onto every schema instance, half of contracts' heap; zod v4 would be worsePerformanceEffort SMedium riskMedium confidence
Where
  • node_modules/zod/v3/types.js:255-288 (zod 3.25.76, ZodType constructor)
  • packages/contracts/package.json:15
  • packages/adapter-claude/package.json (zod 4.4.3 installed nested for the Claude Agent SDK peer)
Evidence

Zod v3's ZodType constructor runs this.parse = this.parse.bind(this) and 23 more binds, plus a ~standard object with a closure, for every instance. With 36,723 instances that is roughly 880,000 function objects allocated at import.

Experiment on a scratch copy of zod 3.25.76 whose constructor only stores _def (methods stay on the prototype; spa and ~standard become getters):

  • Bundled contracts: evaluation 190–220 → 128–156 ms, heap 57 → 29 MB, RSS 152 → 105 MB.
  • The client's contracts slice: 164–178 → 95–103 ms, heap 53 → 25 MB.
  • Same results on four sample frames (two valid, two invalid; data and issue paths compared); a fixture snapshot parsed in 429 µs against 572 µs.
  • A search for detached method use (list.map(Schema.parse), destructured parse) found only type positions such as ReturnType<typeof X.parse>.

Zod v4 benchmark (2,000 strict eight-field objects in one discriminated union, fresh process each): v3 165–207 ms and 46 MB; zod/v4 from 3.25.76 1,038–1,239 ms and 193 MB; zod 4.4.3 classic 708–1,007 ms and 223 MB; zod 4.4.3 mini 316–342 ms and 108 MB. Union parse was 0.5–2.2 µs against v3's 1.3–1.7 µs.

Why it matters

Construction cost and memory scale with the number of schemas defined, not with the number used, and every process constructs all of them (CT-01). Halving the heap matters most where memory is tight: a phone tab through remote access and the Electron renderer. The v4 numbers matter as a warning: a migration undertaken for parse speed would multiply startup cost for this eager-construction style.

Options
  1. AKeep zod v3 and patch out the eager bindsRecommended

    A small patch (patch-package, or an npm overrides entry pointing at a vendored 3.25.76) that leaves methods on the prototype; zod 3.x is frozen at 3.25.76, so the patch will not drift. Add a test that the patch is applied and a lint rule against passing schema methods detached. Run the full suite against it before adopting.

  2. BStatus quo

    Accept about 28 MB of extra heap and about 60 ms per process. No maintenance item.

  3. CMigrate to zod v4 classic or mini

    Not recommended: measured 2–6× slower construction and 1.5–5× the heap for this pattern. Worth revisiting only together with lazy schema construction, which v3 discriminated-union options cannot use anyway.

Impact

About −30% evaluation time and −28 MB heap per process (desktop main, renderer, phone tab, engine host, each test process); roughly 1 CPU-minute per test run per platform (about 1,100 processes × 55 ms). Measured on this container.

Risk

Code that calls a schema method detached from its schema would break; none found in tracked sources, but third-party code receiving our zod v3 instances was not audited and the full test suite was not run against the patched build. A patched dependency is a maintenance item the repository does not have today.

CT-03Each event is zod-validated at emit, again per connection, and again in the clientPerformanceUser journeyEffort SMedium riskMedium confidence
Where
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:4955-4957
  • packages/coordinator/src/transport.ts:373-417
  • packages/coordinator/src/transport.ts:304
  • packages/coordinator/src/remote-access/gateway.ts:252
  • packages/client/src/lib/frame-parser.ts:8-20
  • packages/client/src/lib/store.ts:1789-1800
Evidence
  • emit() parses every event with DomainEventSchema.parse ("Validate, fold, log, broadcast — the one path every event takes (R-3)").
  • broadcast() then calls sendFrame() once per connection, and sendFrame() runs FrameSchema.parse(outgoing) each time: the same event again for every window or paired phone. Snapshots and snapshot pages are also parsed per connection. Only events rewritten for retain-history connections (jobSummary, transport.ts:407) are new data at that point.
  • The client parses every incoming frame again (parseIncomingFrame → FrameSchema.parse, skipping only snapshots' jobs, ledger and artifacts), on the UI thread.
  • Commands from a phone are parsed by the gateway and then by the transport.

Measured (Node 22, tsx): a job.updated event takes 9.5 µs to validate against 1.0 µs to stringify; the client fixture snapshot (11.8 KB) 302 µs against 33 µs; a 315 KB scaled snapshot 4.1 ms against 0.96 ms.

In the client bundle, FrameSchema is what keeps most of the event and state vocabulary alive. With tree-shaking on (CT-01 A), removing the client's FrameSchema use takes its contracts slice from 1,166 to 952 KB minified, evaluation from 141–150 to 97–115 ms and heap from 47 to 31 MB. Combined with CT-02 A the slice evaluates in 64–74 ms with 16 MB, against 164–178 ms and 53 MB today.

Why it matters

The coordinator and the client ship together and the socket is authenticated, so the client's second full validation mostly re-checks the coordinator's own output, on the thread that draws the UI, and phones pay it on slower CPUs. The per-connection re-validation on the coordinator repeats work done a few microseconds earlier at emit, and grows with every paired device.

Options
  1. ATransport validates only what it composesRecommended

    Keep emit()'s parse (the single event path). In sendFrame, validate snapshots, snapshot pages, studio-assistant replies and rewritten job events; send other event frames as already validated. Where several connections receive an identical snapshot payload, validate it once per broadcast. Small change in transport.ts.

  2. BClient checks the envelope, not the whole frame

    Validate kind, seq and event type and the interactive controls the store relies on; run full FrameSchema validation only in development builds or when hello reports a build mismatch. Keeps the schema for tests. Saves about 214 KB of bundle, 45 ms of startup evaluation and 16 MB of heap (desktop-class CPU), plus the per-frame parse.

  3. CKeep all validation

    Defence in depth against a renderer and coordinator from different builds, which in practice happens only in development.

Impact

Coordinator: one fewer full event parse per event per connection (about 9.5 µs each at the measured size) and N−1 fewer snapshot parses with N connections (0.3–4 ms each at the measured sizes). Client with option B: −214 KB minified, about −45 ms and −16 MB at page load, and no per-frame schema walk. Real-world totals depend on snapshot sizes, which were not measured.

Risk

transport.ts states a deliberate rule ('a frame that fails its own schema must never reach a client'); option A keeps it for everything the transport builds and relies on emit's validation for the rest. Relaxing the client (option B) needs a decision against SPEC-001 R-3 and §2.6. Guards: coordinator test/transport.test.ts and client test/frame-parser.test.ts.

Cited specs
SPEC-001 R-3 SPEC-001 §2.6Design records the reviewers could not read; check before changing.
CT-04Export recovery zod-parses every change-log record on the way to the first snapshotPerformanceEffort SLow riskHigh confidence
Where
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:5134-5146
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:4328
  • packages/coordinator/src/coordinator.ts:5943
  • packages/coordinator/src/change-log.ts:21
  • packages/coordinator/src/change-log.ts:158-175
  • packages/coordinator/src/journal-record.ts:13
Evidence

durableExportReads reads both retained change-log generations (the live file rolls at 16 MB and one .old generation is kept; each is read with readTail(path, 32 MB)), JSON-parses every line, then runs DomainEventSchema.safeParse — the full 248-way union — on every record, to keep only export.progress rows for one world. It runs in beforeInitialSnapshot (coordinator.ts:4328) and again after world-open recovery (coordinator.ts:5943).

Synthetic replay of a 16 MB log (37,685 journalled events, 1% export rows): zod work 254–345 ms; with a pre-filter on event.type === "export.progress" && event.worldId === worldId before safeParse, 6–18 ms, keeping the same 377 rows. JSON-parsing the same file took 82–205 ms.

Why it matters

This sits on the path to the first snapshot after start and on every world open, and it grows with use until the log rolls. On a busy install the zod part alone is about a quarter to a third of a second per generation read. This overlaps with the startup reviewer's area and is listed here because it is a parse of the big union where one option suffices.

Options
  1. APre-filter raw records before validatingRecommended

    Check record.event?.type and worldId on the parsed JSON and only then safeParse (or parse with the export.progress option's own schema). Same rows kept; summarised records already fail validation and stay skipped.

  2. BKeep a small export-progress journal

    Write export rows to their own file or index so neither JSON.parse nor zod touches unrelated history. More code, and a second durable record to keep consistent.

Impact

About 240–330 ms less CPU per 16 MB of retained log per call, so up to roughly 0.5–0.7 s when both generations are full, before the first snapshot and on each world open. Measured on synthetic data shaped like the journalled events.

Risk

Behaviour is unchanged for every row that matters. Cover with coordinator test/change-log.test.ts and test/productions/export-receipts.test.ts; no direct test of the interrupted-export replay was found, so add one with the change.

CT-05Fifteen canonical-JSON implementations with at least three different semanticsSimplificationEffort MMedium riskHigh confidence
Where
  • packages/contracts/src/timeline.ts:1158
  • packages/contracts/src/dialogue-assessment.ts:132
  • packages/contracts/src/editor-effect-protection.ts:50
  • packages/contracts/src/production-readiness.ts:63-91
  • packages/contracts/src/editor-effect-analysis.ts:104
  • packages/coordinator/src/productions/timeline.ts:109
  • packages/coordinator/src/arke-actions/digest.ts:3
  • packages/coordinator/src/application/operations.ts:4
  • packages/coordinator/src/productions/editor-effect-requests.ts:169
  • packages/coordinator/src/publications/video.ts:51
  • packages/coordinator/src/world-chat/readiness.ts:235
  • packages/client/src/components/timeline-card-history.tsx:6-14
  • packages/client/src/screens/scene-workspace/stage.tsx:1588
  • packages/providers/src/comfyui/recipes.ts:760
  • packages/adapter-opencode/src/v2/private-destination.ts:17
Evidence

Fifteen private or near-private "stable JSON" serialisers feed digests, fingerprints and equality checks. They differ in ways that change output:

  • Key order: code-unit order in most; localeCompare (host-collation dependent) in production-readiness.ts (the production-export-v1: fingerprint), adapter-opencode's private destination and the client's stage draft comparison. coordinator digest.ts carries the warning itself: "Code-unit order is identical on every host; locale collation is not."
  • Undefined members: dropped by most; written as null by editor-effect-protection.ts ({a: undefined} becomes {"a":null}).
  • Unsupported top-level values: "null" (operations.ts), undefined (several), or a thrown error (effectAnalysisCanonicalJson).

Two pairs are copies: the 12-line canonical in contracts timeline.ts:1158 and coordinator productions/timeline.ts:109 are textually identical, and the client's stableJson (timeline-card-history.tsx) matches coordinator digest.ts. Some must agree across the wire: the client compares historyEntryDigest(entry) with action.receipt.digest produced by the coordinator (timeline-card-history.tsx:24), and the coordinator produces history digests with yet other copies (productions/timeline.ts:408, editor-effect-requests.ts:500).

Why it matters

When two implementations that must agree drift, nothing fails loudly: a receipt simply stops matching and the card's history control disappears, or a fingerprint reports a delivered production as stale. One documented function per algorithm makes every digest's rules findable and testable.

Options
  1. AOne canonicalJson in contracts, adopted where output is byte-identicalRecommended

    Promote effectAnalysisCanonicalJson's semantics (code-unit key order, drop undefined members, throw on unsupported values) to a general canonicalJson with golden tests. Switch the copies whose output is provably identical first (the timeline pair, the stableJson pair, editor-effect-requests). Move the locale-ordered and null-writing variants beside it under explicit names with tests pinning today's output, because they feed persisted identities.

  2. BLeave the copies; test the pairs that cross the wire

    Add equality tests between client and coordinator digests. Cheaper, keeps 15 implementations.

Impact

Removes about ten private copies (roughly 60–80 lines) and puts every digest algorithm in one module; prevents silent client/coordinator digest drift. Estimated by counting the implementations found.

Risk

Changing an algorithm that feeds a persisted identity changes hashes on disk: production-export-v1: fingerprints, publication video digests (SPEC-048), ComfyUI recipe identities (pinned recipes) and timeline history digests. Replace only where outputs are proven byte-identical (property tests including undefined, nested arrays and integer-like keys); version any algorithm that must change.

Cited specs

CT-06The ClientState event fold is written twice, arm for arm, in the coordinator and the clientSimplificationUser journeyEffort MMedium riskHigh confidence
Where
  • packages/coordinator/src/read-model.ts:253-530
  • packages/client/src/lib/store.ts:1586-1760
  • packages/client/src/lib/store.ts:1716-1729
  • packages/coordinator/src/read-model.ts:466-480
Evidence

The coordinator's read model has case arms for 79 event types (some deliberate no-ops) in the server's ClientState; the client's pure fold(state, event) has 46, and all 46 also appear in the read model, many line for line on the same contracts types (for example job.updated, ledger.appended, storage.health, narrator.changed, selection.changed).

A client comment records the failure mode this invites: "Folded late (2026-08-26): without this arm the absent → signing-in → ready progression only ever arrived by reconnect snapshot, so the row could not move while you watched."

Two of the duplicated arms, entity.changed and canon.revision.advanced, fold events that no source file emits (see CT-08), so the same dead code exists in both packages.

Why it matters

A fold added on one side only leaves the window and the coordinator disagreeing until the next snapshot, which the user sees as a control that does not move. A single pure reducer used by both makes that impossible and removes about 150 duplicated lines.

Options
  1. AMove the shared fold into contractsRecommended

    The client's fold is already pure; move the shared arms to contracts as foldClientState(state, event) and have ReadModel.apply call it first, keeping server-only arms (world list, export reads, genesis bookkeeping) in the read model. Diff each arm before merging.

  2. BKeep both and test that they agree

    A contract test that replays every event type through both folds and compares the shared part of the state. Catches drift without removing code.

  3. CStatus quo

    The 2026-08-04 audit called client-side folding intentional; options A and B keep client folding and only share or check the reducer.

Impact

About 150 lines removed from read-model.ts (46 overlapping arms) and a structural guarantee that both sides apply an event the same way. Estimated by counting the overlapping case arms.

Risk

Some arms may differ on purpose (retain-history job summaries, world guards). Guards: coordinator test/read-model.test.ts and the four client tests that use __applyForTest. Check SPEC-001 §2.6, which defines the read model.

Cited specs

CT-07A command that fails its schema is dropped with no reply, and many UI limits are copied by handUser journeySimplificationEffort SLow riskMedium confidence
Where
  • packages/coordinator/src/transport.ts:303-313
  • packages/coordinator/src/remote-access/gateway.ts:252-258
  • packages/contracts/src/frames.ts:103-109
  • packages/client/src/lib/store.ts:3346-3356
  • packages/client/src/screens/scene-workspace/stage.tsx:1756
  • packages/contracts/src/remote-access.ts:42-45
Evidence

Valid JSON that fails ClientMessageSchema is logged ("dropping a client message this build does not understand") and dropped; nothing is sent back, and the phone gateway drops it the same way. The client sends commands typed as ClientMessage but never checks runtime bounds (lengths, uuids, patterns, ranges) — it does not import ClientMessageSchema — so a value past a bound produces silence.

Contracts already describes the consequence for one case: "a frame past them is refused without an answer, and a screen holding its controls for one would wait for ever" (PASSAGE_SPAN_MAX, frames.ts). Bounds reach the UI in two ways: 20 maxLength attributes use named constants, most of them contracts exports (SHORT_NAME_MAX, PERFORMANCE_NOTE_MAX, CHAPTER_PLAN_LIMITS...), while 56 of the 76 repeat numbers by hand, for example the stage instruction's maxLength={4000} mirroring instruction: z.string().max(4000). frames.ts has 245 lines with literal .max(n) bounds.

Why it matters

When a hand-copied limit drifts from its schema, or a field has no limit in the UI, the user's action vanishes: a spinner keeps spinning or a control stays locked, with no message. A correlated refusal turns that into an immediate, explained failure.

Options
  1. AReply with a correlated refusalRecommended

    When a message that names a known kind (or carries a requestId) fails the schema, answer with a refusal frame, extending the existing command-refused shape with refused: "invalid" and the request id, so the screen can release its controls and show plain copy. Keep dropping unknown kinds silently for version skew.

  2. BExport command bounds as named constants

    Follow the PASSAGE_SPAN_MAX and SHORT_NAME_MAX pattern for every user-entered field in a command schema and use the constants in the inputs. Small per field.

  3. CValidate outgoing commands in the client

    Not recommended: it pulls all 556 command schemas into the browser bundle and its startup.

Impact

Turns indefinite waits into an explained refusal; removes up to 56 hand-copied limits (count of literal maxLength values in client src).

Risk

Keep the drop-and-continue rule for unknown kinds (the transport's 2026-08-22 review note). Guard with coordinator test/transport.test.ts and a client test for the refusal path. Check SPEC-001 R-3 on frame sequencing: a refusal must not consume or reset event sequence numbers, as the existing gateway refusal already avoids.

CT-08Dead surface: unused exports, never-emitted events and commands with no senderSimplificationEffort SLow riskHigh confidence
Where
  • packages/contracts/src/index.ts:1-260
  • packages/contracts/src/dispatch-plan.ts:242-338
  • packages/coordinator/src/productions/plans.ts:72-95
  • packages/contracts/src/spine.ts:110-135
  • packages/contracts/src/spine.ts:436-640
  • packages/coordinator/src/productions/story-export.ts:94-98

  • packages/coordinator/src/read-model.ts:503
  • packages/coordinator/src/arke-actions/registry.ts:474
Evidence

Exports. The barrel exports 4,636 names. 1,291 runtime values (42%) and 582 types are imported by no other package: 513 are used only by other contracts modules, 579 only inside their own file, 187 only by tests and 12 by nothing.

Dead code (reference graph from every name another package's src imports):

  • 19 value declarations (139 lines) no shipped code can reach, led by PlanEventSchema (93 lines). Plan events are meanwhile written untyped and read back as JSON.parse(line) as PlanEventLike.
  • 54 value declarations (about 579 lines) reached only from tests: the LRC lyric import (parseLrc 156 lines, markersFromImport, three import schemas; about 217 lines in spine.ts, issue #253), lockedDurationEstimate, keyframeSequence, boardPackKey, stagingBeats, and storyRoutes, whose walk the coordinator's story exporter re-implements ("It walks as storyRoutes does").
  • About 200 type aliases and interfaces that nothing references.

Events: 248 types, 243 handled by the client. world.closed, entity.changed and canon.revision.advanced are never constructed in any src file, yet the read model folds all three and the client folds the latter two. proposal.staged, sample-world.installed and sample-world.refused and probe.grouped-read are emitted but no client code handles them (the sample-world outcome also reaches the snapshot).

Commands: 556 kinds; 21 have no sender in client or desktop source. 13 of them are Arke agent actions. Of the 8 marked human-only in the Arke registry, 4 are character-audio commands that CLAUDE.md says deliberately have no consumer UI yet (issue #117) and one is a script probe; proposal-update-field, propose-shot-visual-facts and draft-scene have handlers and registry entries but no UI that sends them.

Why it matters

Each unused declaration is something a reader has to understand and a refactor has to carry; never-emitted events have fold code in two packages; handlers without a sender are untested paths in the 25,000-line coordinator. The runtime saving is small; the clarity gain is not.

Options
  1. ADelete what is provably dead and decide the test-only featuresRecommended

    Delete the 19 unreachable declarations and the three never-emitted events with their five fold arms. For each test-only feature decide wire-or-delete (LRC import; storyRoutes against the exporter's own walk). Either type appendPlanEvents with z.infer<typeof PlanEventSchema> (and safeParse on read, skipping bad lines as R-10 requires) or delete the schema. Confirm the three sender-less commands with the owner.

  2. BAdd an export-usage check to CI

    Run the census script (or knip) so a new export no package imports, or an event nobody emits, fails review.

  3. CDrop export from names used only in their own file

    579 names; cosmetic, shrinks the public surface by about 19% with no behaviour change.

Impact

About 720 lines of value code and about 200 types removed; three event schemas and five duplicated fold arms; fewer than a thousand fewer zod instances, so a negligible runtime saving.

Risk

Removing an event type makes old change-log rows of that type fail to parse; the one replay (durableExportReads) already skips unknown rows. Removing commands changes the wire vocabulary: check the three sender-less ones against SPEC-050 R-7..R-10 and SPEC-051 R-46..R-48 (the Arke registry's contract), and leave the issue #117 audio commands alone. Check SPEC-024 R-9..R-11 before touching PlanEventSchema.

CT-09Two scene shapes and a cut.json fold still run on main paths behind 'legacy' namesSimplificationEffort MMedium riskMedium confidence
Where

Evidence

SceneRecord is either a legacy linear Scene (with shots[]) or a GraphScene (with flow). New scenes are made by passing an empty legacy scene through migrateLegacyScene({ ..., shots: [] }) in four coordinator creation paths. Five client screens (seven call sites: development, production-generate, production-takes, shot-page, workspace) read scenes through legacySceneView, which its own comment calls "a read-only legacy-shaped compatibility view for APIs and fixtures that still consume Scene. New code should consume the SceneRecord or its ordered sequence directly."

migrateLegacyCut (176 lines) runs on every timeline read in both packages (3 client and 8 coordinator call sites), including for brand-new productions (migrateLegacyCut(seedFirstPictureTimeline(production), ...)), so the "migration" is in fact the current read path. Declarations with legacy or migration names in contracts total about 370 lines, and 52 contracts modules mention legacy or migration handling.

Why it matters

Every new scene round-trips through a shape the code says nobody should use, and readers cannot tell which 'legacy' code guards old worlds on disk and which is simply the way things work now. That makes the genuinely retirable compatibility code impossible to find.

Options
  1. AStop creating and reading through the legacy shapes; isolate the true readersRecommended

    Add newGraphScene(...) for the four creation paths (same deterministic ids), move the five screens to orderedShots(record), rename the fold that runs on every timeline read, and keep the old-record readers together in one module.

  2. BSet a minimum supported world schema and migrate once

    Ship a one-time upgrade that rewrites linear scenes and cut.json placements, then delete the readers for worlds below the minimum. Large; needs a product decision, because worlds on users' disks must keep opening.

  3. CStatus quo

    Works; the cost is comprehension.

Impact

Removes the legacy round trip for every new scene and seven client renders; puts about 370 lines of compatibility code in one place where its retirement can be planned. No meaningful runtime change.

Risk

Worlds on users' disks must keep opening, so the readers stay until a migration and minimum version exist. migrateLegacyScene is documented as deterministic (byte-identical flow, same ids); a new constructor must keep that. Check SPEC-029 R-1, R-7, R-11, R-12 and SPEC-037 R-30, R-31 / SPEC-038 R-12, R-20.

Client · CS · 11 findings

Client state management, data flow, rendering and loading performance

The store's foundations are sound: a module singleton read through useSyncExternalStore, structural sharing of snapshots, paged history and a selector hook with equality. But most of the app subscribes to everything: the routes component, both layouts and the shared picture tile re-render on every event, so one unrelated job or progress event re-renders 71-86% of a screen and costs 24-37 ms on a 2,000-item Artifacts shelf in Chrome; one-line selector changes in five files cut that by 77-92% in a measured simulation. Loading is the second lever: one 5.86 MB chunk (9.4x August's), with three.js pulled into start-up by the root-level chat, served to phones uncompressed and uncached (6.6 s versus 2.2 s on a throttled link). store.ts (8,133 lines, a reducer duplicated in the coordinator, 93 hand-written channels) should be split behind a barrel, and a Rules-of-Hooks violation that crashes the audiobook requests panel on disconnect should be fixed with the lint rule switched on.

How this area is built, and how it was reviewed

The client is a thin projection of coordinator state. lib/store.ts owns a module-level current: StoreState and a bridge (the Electron preload, or a WebSocket in development and on paired phones). A snapshot frame is parsed by frame-parser.ts (zod for everything except the artifact, job and ledger arrays, which arrive as already-validated pages through SnapshotPageBuffer), merged by shareSnapshot so unchanged branches keep their identity, and combined with per-slice rules for what a world change or a rejoin clears. An event frame is folded by fold (46 event types that change ClientState, as immutable spread updates) and by a 1,456-line branch that updates 69 client-only slices (live run progress, request and answer correlation, refusals) and calls 93 hand-written listener sets. Either way emitChange installs a new root and calls every subscriber synchronously.

Components read through useSyncExternalStore: useStore() returns the whole root, useStoreSelector(selector, equals) a cached slice, and 67 exported use* functions wrap one or the other (five of them are commands, not hooks). Derived views live in lib/selectors.ts and in render bodies; there is one React.memo, no React Compiler and no list virtualisation. App.tsx declares 100 routes over 40 statically imported screen modules under GlobalChatProvider, which keeps the selected conversation mounted app-wide. Vite (target chrome120, base './', no manual chunks) emits one 5.86 MB script and one 1.29 MB stylesheet; the only dynamic import is the PDF preview. Electron loads that bundle from file://, and the coordinator's remote gateway serves it to paired phones.

Scope and method

Read CLAUDE.md, the root and client AGENTS.md, the code map's startup, state-ownership and large-snapshot rows, testing.md's snapshot section and the four earlier audits. Examined client lib/ (store.ts structure throughout, frame-parser, snapshot-pages, selectors, theme, media-query, playback-engine), App.tsx, main.tsx, vite.config.ts, the global chat, Portrait, the card components, the Artifacts screen and the 3D stage. Counts come from git grep and awk over packages/client/src. All measurements ran from scratch folders; nothing in the repository was edited:

  • linkedom with React's development build: mounted the real App on 9 routes with the test fixture and counted re-rendered components per event through a React DevTools commit hook using DevTools' own rule.
  • Simulated fixes in memory (a Node loader hook and an esbuild onLoad patch) for before and after comparisons.
  • Headless Chrome 153 (production React, all CSS, forced layout, 15 events per case, two runs), adapted from scripts/benchmark-client-snapshots.mjs.
  • Start-up of the BUILD-CI reviewer's build of HEAD, served read-only, with CPU and network throttling and gzip on or off.
  • Source-map attribution of that build plus a static import graph, to estimate lazy-boundary savings.
  • Node timings of the frame-parser functions, and oxlint's react/rules-of-hooks run read-only.

Not covered: screen and component structure and CSS content (another reviewer), the bundle build itself, coordinator transport internals, the Electron runtime, physical phones or Tailscale, and GPU profiling of the stage.

Findings

CS-01Every store event re-renders almost the whole visible screenPerformanceSimplificationEffort SLow riskHigh confidence
Where
  • packages/client/src/App.tsx:240
  • packages/client/src/lib/theme.ts:108-126
  • packages/client/src/lib/selectors.ts:50-58
  • packages/client/src/components/world-open-refusal.tsx:21-26
  • packages/client/src/screens/production-story.tsx:93
  • packages/client/src/screens/production-story.tsx:131
  • packages/client/src/lib/store.ts:1566-1583
  • packages/client/src/lib/store.ts:3174-3242
  • packages/client/src/lib/store.ts:7224-7239
Evidence

The store is a module singleton read through useSyncExternalStore, and a selector hook with equality already exists (useStoreSelector, store.ts:7229). The common path still subscribes to everything:

  • useStore() returns the whole StoreState, and emitChange installs a new root on every snapshot and every event. The event branch always builds { ...current, ... } (store.ts:3174), even for events whose only effect is a listener callback (production-narrative.saved, dialogue.result, chapter.save-result; 86 of the 95 dispatches in handleFrame are one-line callbacks).
  • 207 direct useStore() calls in 130 files, plus about 95 call sites that subscribe through shared hooks without saying so: 74 via useOpenWorldGuard/useSheet/useProduction (selectors.ts:51 reads only connection), 18 via seven store hooks built on useStore() (useSetup, useEnvCheck, useProviderCalls, useWorldChatRefusals, useWorldChatWrapUpRefusal, useWorldChatRipples, useWorldChatProgress) and 3 via useThemePreference. Selector-based reads: 164 sites.
  • AppRoutes calls useThemePreference() (App.tsx:240), which calls useStore() (theme.ts:109). The component that renders <Routes> therefore re-renders on every store change; its route elements are new React elements each time, so the matched layout and screen re-render top-down. The client has one memo() (queue-toaster.tsx:118) and no React Compiler.

Measured with a scratch harness that mounts the real App on the test fixture and counts re-rendered components per commit with React DevTools' own rule: one unrelated event (listener-only, a world-chat.progress for another conversation, a background job.updated, or an unchanged snapshot) re-rendered world overview 71/92 components, cast 79/100, production dashboard 86/111, chapter 73/95, scene detail 216/304, Generate 151/176, world picker 47/66 — always including AppRoutes.

Simulating the fix in memory (five shared hooks select only what they read: useThemePreference, useOpenWorldGuard, useWorldOpenRefusal, useNewScene, useNewChapter) cut those counts to 26, 27, 35, 22, 168, 104 and 34 for the listener-only and progress events.

Why it matters

Snapshots arrive up to four times a second while work runs (the coordinator coalesces them at 250 ms, transport.ts:421-427) with job, progress and run events between them. Each one re-runs every render function on screen and the derivations inside them (CS-10), so cost scales with screen and world size rather than with what changed.

It also defeats the selectors already written for the chapter, audiobook and Bench (code map, 'Large snapshot rendering'): they hold, but their parents re-render them anyway. The repo benchmark cannot see this because it mounts ChapterScreen outside App (CS-11).

Options
  1. AMake the shared hooks and the app shell select what they readRecommended

    Add useConnection() and change the five shared hooks (about ten lines). AppRoutes and both layouts then re-render only for their own fields; values returned are identical.

    export const useConnection = () => useStoreSelector(s => s.connection);
// lib/selectors.ts, useOpenWorldGuard
const connection = useConnection();
// lib/theme.ts, useThemePreference
const authority = useStoreSelector(s => s.state?.app.appearance.theme);
  2. BDo not publish a root that did not changeRecommended

    In handleFrame's event branch, run settleHolds first, then compare the next store with current field by field and skip emitChange when all 71 fields are identical. Callback-only events become free for every subscriber. settleHolds must run before the comparison because it reads the module-level sendResults map (store.ts:1395, 2966).

The paired-device gateway serves the built client itself. Why it matters

On a phone over Tailscale every cold open and every reload pays the full transfer, because nothing may be cached; on a slow link the launch surface needs seconds before it can even say it is connecting. The Electron file page reads local files, which is why this has gone unnoticed.

  2. BCompress text assetsRecommended

    The page already registers notification-worker.js; a precache would allow offline start but couples to the update flow. Unnecessary once A and B are in.

Cross-cutting with the runtime/remote-access reviewer. The gateway calls the shell public, and CLAUDE.md forbids the capability in public HTML, URLs it is removed from and build-time VITE_* variables, so hashed assets carry no secret; still check against SPEC-001 §2.5 and the remote-access guide before relaxing no-store, and keep it on the shell, /remote/* and media. Regressions: coordinator test/remote-access.test.ts, desktop scripts/smoke-remote-access.mjs. A new shell cannot request an old chunk because names change with content.

    export function lazyRoute<P extends object>(load: () => Promise<ComponentType<P>>) {
  let loaded: ComponentType<P> | null = null;
  const preload = () => load().then(c => (loaded = c));
  const Lazy = lazy(() => preload().then(c => ({ default: c })));
  const Route = (props: P) => createElement(loaded ?? Lazy, props);
  return Object.assign(Route, { preload });
}

The dev server requests about 180-200 fewer client modules before the launch screen (441 eager today).

    type Of<T extends DomainEvent["type"]> = Extract<DomainEvent, { type: T }>;
const channels = new Map<string, Set<(event: never) => void>>();
export function onEvent<T extends DomainEvent["type"]>(type: T, fn: (event: Of<T>) => void) {
  const set = channels.get(type) ?? new Set(); channels.set(type, set);
  set.add(fn as (event: never) => void); return () => void set.delete(fn as (event: never) => void);
}

Check against SPEC-001 §2.6 (the read model's role) and the frame-run requirement before choosing which production.frame-run behaviour is right; do not guess. Tests: client tests using __applyForTest, coordinator read-model and transport tests.

  • acceptedTakeId (17 call sites) filters all of a production's takes through takesForShot on each call, and reviewableTakesForShot adds a find over takes per take; called per shot that is shots x takes per render. takeDecisions rebuilds a map of all takes and reviews in three render paths without a memo.
  • 24 .artifacts. scans (find, filter, map and similar) in .tsx files run during render, several inside loops (episode-script.tsx:501, comic-pages.tsx:481). There is no shared artifact or take index.

  • useMediaQuery (130 call sites) calls window.matchMedia(query), creating a new MediaQueryList, on every read.
Why it matters

Each is cheap alone; multiplied by whole-tree re-renders (CS-01) and by world size they set the per-event floor the Chrome numbers show.

Options
  1. ACache derived indexes by collection identityRecommended

    Structural sharing keeps world.artifacts, production.takes and state.app.jobs identical until they change, so a WeakMap keyed by the array gives constant-time repeat lookups: artifactById(world), takesByShot(production), and needsYouCount(state) as a selector.

  2. BDo CS-01 first and re-measure

    Once only changed subtrees render, several of these stop mattering; memoise what the profile still shows.

  3. CCache one MediaQueryList per queryRecommended

    A module-level map in media-query.ts; reads become a property access.

Impact

Take lookups drop from shots x takes to shots per render and artifact lookups from linear to constant after the first call (complexity estimate; not measured on a large production).

Risk

Pure caches keyed by immutable arrays invalidate themselves, because shareSnapshot and the fold never mutate a published array. If the needs-you computation moves, check it against SPEC-014 R-20 to R-27.

Evidence

Each snapshot (at most one per 250 ms per connection) is JSON.parsed, run through FrameSchema.parse for everything except the artifact, job and ledger arrays (frame-parser.ts:8-21), then deep-walked by shareSnapshot. The coordinator already validates every frame it sends (transport.ts:379, 385, 409). Timing the client functions in Node on the test fixture scaled by production count: zod about 26 ms per MB, JSON.parse 3.3 ms per MB, shareSnapshot 6 ms per MB (a 215 KiB snapshot: 5.6, 0.7 and 1.3 ms).

scripts/benchmark-client-snapshots.mjs mounts ChapterScreen alone in a MemoryRouter, so it measures the chapter's own selectors but not the AppRoutes cascade (CS-01) that dominates in the real app.

Why it matters

Zod is about three quarters of non-React ingestion. At four snapshots a second with 1 MB of non-collection state that is about 140 ms per second of main thread on this machine before React renders anything (estimate), more on phones. And without an app-level benchmark the CS-01 fix can regress unnoticed.

Options
  1. AMeasure the real shape firstRecommended

    Extend the benchmark to mount App at a few routes and replay events, and record the non-collection snapshot size of real worlds.

  2. BValidate what changed

    Validate fully on the first snapshot after hello, then only top-level branches whose content changed. Schema defaults mean raw and parsed trees differ, so this needs care.

  3. CParse off the main thread

    A worker runs JSON.parse and zod and posts the result; the structured clone back costs roughly another parse. Helps phones most.

Impact

B would take up to about 26 ms per MB per snapshot off the main thread (measured cost of the skipped step); C moves about 36 ms per MB. A has no runtime effect but protects CS-01.

Risk

frame-parser.ts states the trade-off on purpose (validate the envelope and interactive state, trust the authenticated coordinator for history rows), and client validation is the version-skew guard that drops bad frames loudly: keep full validation on connect and in development. Paged snapshots and reconnect sequencing stay as they are. Tests: client test/frame-parser.test.ts, snapshot-pages.test.ts, snapshot-history.test.ts.

No findings in this area match the filters.

  • CS-02 In Portrait, replace useStore() with useStoreSelector(s => s.state?.app.adapters?.adultContent.enabled === true).
  • CS-03 Hoist useProductionReading above the || in BookRequests, then enable react/rules-of-hooks in .oxlintrc.json and clear the other four errors.
  • CS-04 In the gateway, send Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable for /assets/* only, keep no-store elsewhere, and gzip text assets.
  • CS-01 Skip emitChange in the event branch when the next store is field-for-field identical to current after settleHolds.
  • CS-11 Point benchmark-client-snapshots.mjs at the full App on a few routes, and add a useStore() count ratchet to scripts/check-client-policy.mjs.

Client · CU · 15 findings

Client UI: screens, components and styling - structure and duplication

The client UI has good shared foundations (a documented dialog system of BodyLayer, PageSheet, EditorDialog and overlays.ts; a shared Composer and production conversation used at 9 and 16 sites; token files guarded byte for byte), but it is held together by convention more than structure: 46 surfaces hand-roll dialogs or popovers beside the three shared primitives, several flows (voice-upload consent at five sites, streamed read-aloud at two, the picture and crossfade review pair, a chat composer) re-implement a shared hook or component that already exists, and the best implementations of a menu, a tab strip and a commit-on-blur field live inside screen files, hard-wired to one feature, where other screens do not reach them. All 23,092 lines of CSS form one global, order-dependent cascade dominated by a 9,051-line fidelity.css, with one control restyled in up to 36 files, about 395 rules that can never match, and type and spacing tokens largely bypassed although comments say otherwise. About 660 lines of UI, including the whole Propose-timing flow, have no product caller and survive only because tests render them. The cheapest high-value moves are deleting the orphans and dead CSS, moving the shared kits out of screens, naming breakpoints and adding one lint ratchet on hand-rolled overlays; the large-file splits should follow issue 101's pure-move method.

How this area is built, and how it was reviewed

Routes are declared in App.tsx, which imports every screen eagerly; a HashRouter lets one bundle run from Vite, file:// and the packaged app. screens/ holds route bodies and, increasingly, feature modules: 154 TS/TSX files and 75.7k lines, with the scene workspace in its own folder and the video editor laid out flat as 44 editor-* modules beside cut.tsx. components/ (185 files, 33k lines) holds shared UI: the ui.tsx primitives (Button, Input, Select, Switch, Callout, Badge), layout.tsx (Screen, Section, EmptyState), the dialog system (BodyLayer, PageSheet, EditorDialog, ResponsiveSheet, ordered by lib/overlays.ts), Composer, the production conversation and many feature cards. domain/ renders proposals and gate decisions. Components mostly read the whole store through useStore() and receive whole world and production bundles as props.

Styling is plain global CSS: 93 stylesheets imported in a fixed order from main.tsx and never from components, so the node test runner can import components without a CSS loader. The token files are copied byte for byte from design-system/_ds and guarded by check-client-policy.mjs. fidelity.css is the pattern language transcribed from the design prototype; later sheets named for design turns (the *-responsive.css files for turns 168-175, quiet.css for 192, chapter-room.css for 227, arke-half.css for 202) re-dress its rules by cascade order. Prefixes separate areas: fy-, ui-, lay-, scr-, dom-, bm-, xf-/fx-, ij-.

design-system/ (503 tracked files, about 127 MB) is the design record: the master HTML, per-turn review pages and their generators. Lint checks the master's turn ledger and type-token rule, that generated review pages are current, and that hand-listed control labels appear in drawn frames. 15 smoke-*-layout scripts render real components in a headless browser at phone, Fold7 and desktop sizes, most of them against master frames; of the 35 smoke scripts only one runs in CI.

Scope and method

Read-only review at HEAD 42d3def of packages/client/src/screens (154 TS/TSX files including scene-workspace), components (185), domain, theme, all 93 client stylesheets, main.tsx and App.tsx, the three design-system scripts (check-master.mjs, build-review.mjs, build-publish-review.mjs) and scripts/check-client-policy.mjs. Counts come from git grep and small Node scripts kept in the scratch folder scripts/: fnmap.sh (declaration line ranges), dead-classes.mjs and dead-rules.mjs (unreferenced selectors and never-matching rules), exports.mjs and importers.mjs (unused exports and modules), props.mjs (prop widths), dup-blocks.mjs, media-lines.mjs and touch44.mjs. Samples were re-checked by hand (21 of the dead class names, every dialog site cited).

Earlier audits: 2026-08-04 architecture-reuse covered coordinator layering and rated DRY clean at architecture level, not UI duplication; the 2026-09-01 editor gap asked for proper dialogs and focus handling, which was acted on in EditorDialog (Tab trap, EDITOR_KEYS) but not across the app; issue 101 (production.tsx split) was implemented on 2026-09-13 and its issue-1160 follow-up landed (production-takes, production-voice-line, production-episode-picker, production-dashboard, lib/take-presentation.ts exist), while cut.tsx, kept 'for now' at 1,709 lines, is 1,905 today; the 2026-09-05 documentation audit's packages/client/AGENTS.md exists.

Not covered: store and data flow, loading performance and bundle size (another reviewer), journey step counts (two others), coordinator and contracts. I did not build, launch the app, run tests or run the Chrome smoke scripts, and the private specifications were not available, so SPEC and design-turn citations are flagged for checking rather than interpreted.

Findings

CU-01Dialogs, sheets and popovers: three shared primitives, 46 hand-rolled surfacesSimplificationUser journeyEffort LMedium riskHigh confidence
Where
