Evidence

The documented dialog system (code-map.md row 'A dialog, sheet or self-placed menu'; testing.md 'Dialogs and sheets') is BodyLayer, PageSheet (native <dialog> with focus return and nesting), EditorDialog (body-drawn div with a Tab trap) and ResponsiveSheet, ordered by lib/overlays.ts. They are used 113 times: PageSheet 68 in 44 files, EditorDialog 37 in 32, ResponsiveSheet 8 in 6.

Beside them (git grep, comments excluded by hand):

  • 15 native <dialog> elements with their own showModal/onCancel/backdrop code: artifact-viewer, audio-drama-sound, generation-dialog, image-dialog, reference-picker, editor-transitions, production-shell (drawer) and eight in scene-workspace (board-sheet, cast-picker, character-dialog, frame-run, lightbox, location-dialog, rows, shot-page). The mount effect if (node.showModal !== undefined) node.showModal(); else node.setAttribute("open", "") is repeated verbatim in location-dialog.tsx:29, cast-picker.tsx:90, lightbox.tsx:109 and board-sheet.tsx:143.
  • 9 role="dialog" aria-modal="true" divs with their own scrim: audiobook.tsx:935, audiobook-credits.tsx:172, audiobook-player, audiobook-pictures-sheet, interactive-player, voice-picker, remote-voice-upload-confirmation, shell.tsx:555 (archive sheet) and the App.tsx update transition.
  • 22 more role="dialog" surfaces without aria-modal: about ten popovers (adapter-picker, bench-upscale, model-chip x2, bench duration, chapter-ask, chapter-audiobook notes, chapter-names, chapter-workspace voice, stage-plate) and twelve sheets (character-voice catalogue, clone-voice-dialog, character-voice-sample, bench lyrics and brief windows, comic read and mode, world-guide panel and preview, guide teaser picker, line-doors x2).
  • 25 document/window outside-click listeners in 18 files. adapter-picker.tsx:25-38 and bench-upscale.tsx:95-108 are the same 14 lines. The most complete version, usePopover (chapter-audiobook.tsx:2164, captured Escape, focus back to the press, arrow keys) with ToolMenu and MenuPress, sits inside a 4,039-line screen file, so nothing else uses it.

Only page-sheet, editor-dialog and voice-picker call useOverlay, so about 40 surfaces sit outside the stacking order overlays.ts was written for (its header records a sheet that 'could not be pressed'). Behaviour differs per surface: RemoteVoiceUploadConfirmation is aria-modal with no Escape, no focus move and no Tab trap, is drawn in place with position: fixed (fidelity.css:3450) rather than through BodyLayer, and is mounted at 12 sites; clone-voice-dialog, character-voice-sample and line-doors have no Escape handler of their own.

Why it matters

Every bespoke surface re-decides Escape, backdrop, focus and stacking, and the differences reach keyboard and screen-reader users (a modal that cannot be dismissed with Escape, focus left on the page behind an aria-modal layer). The documented rule that every window-wide layer is drawn on the body is only partly true, and that is exactly the clipping bug class BodyLayer exists for. New surfaces copy the nearest example, so the count keeps growing.

Options
  1. AKeep two primitives, add one modal hook and one popover hook, route bespoke surfaces to themRecommended

    Pure-move usePopover, ToolMenu and MenuPress from chapter-audiobook.tsx to components/menu.tsx, let usePopover register a 'layer' with overlays.ts, and replace the 25 outside-click effects. Add a ~30-line useModalDialog(open) (guarded showModal/close, onCancel, backdrop, overlays registration) for the 15 native dialogs. Move the 9 aria-modal divs into PageSheet (side sheets through className). Rename EditorDialog, since 28 of its 30 importers are outside the editor. Work in batches of 5-8 surfaces with smoke-dialog-overlays.mjs and test/sheet-stacking.test.tsx after each batch.

  2. BOne Dialog component with variants (centred, bottom sheet, side sheet, popover)

    Merge PageSheet and EditorDialog behind one API. Cleanest end state, but the two use different DOM (top-layer <dialog> versus a body div) and tests depend on both (test/dialog-root.ts). Larger change and higher regression risk; a sensible later step after A.

  3. CAdopt a headless library (Radix, React Aria)

    Solves focus, stacking and dismissal generically but adds a dependency and a second styling contract, and would compete with overlays.ts and the design turns that specify these sheets. Not recommended.

Impact

Estimated 600-900 lines removed: 25 outside-click effects at 12-20 lines, 15 dialog set-ups at 8-15 lines and 9 scrim/Escape/focus blocks at 15-30 lines (block sizes measured on five samples), replaced by usePopover (52 lines, already written) and a ~30-line hook. About 40 surfaces gain one Escape, focus and stacking behaviour.

Risk

Focus return and nesting are subtle (PageSheet's preserveReturnFocus, modeless for the Fold7 half). Guarded by test/sheet-stacking.test.tsx, tests using test/dialog-root.ts, settings-sheet, clone-voice-flow and editor-target tests, and the manual scripts/smoke-dialog-overlays.mjs and smoke-audiobook-overlays.mjs. Check against SPEC-039 R-5 (editor sheets), SPEC-042 R-5/R-6 (Settings as a sheet), SPEC-046 R-16/R-17 (upload consent) and design turns 150, 163 and 202 before changing what a surface looks like.

Why it matters

Tests that render orphaned components keep them 'used', so ordinary dead-code signals never fire and the code and its CSS keep being maintained and refactored. In the Propose-timing case a feature with its own design turn silently lost its entry point while its tests stayed green.

    Move the components to a test fixture or rename them __...ForTest. Cheap, but keeps about 400 lines of UI that nobody can open.

About 660 TSX lines and 120 CSS lines removed (spans from declaration line ranges), about 20 test cases in chapter-timing.test.tsx retired or rewritten, one stale code-map row fixed; storyboard.tsx loses a quarter of its length and its remaining parts can move to components/ (CU-11).

Typecheck catches any missed caller. The only judgement is the timing view: check against SPEC-047 R-80 to R-88 (R-86 is Propose timing) and design turns 187a/187b. The live parts of chapter-timing.tsx (BlockTimingPanel, SecondsField, useMixPlayer, chapterTimingOf, barAt) stay.

Evidence

Method (scratch dead-classes.mjs and dead-rules.mjs): collect every class selector in the 93 client stylesheets (5,295 distinct names in 12,827 rules). A class is live if any client .ts, .tsx or .html file contains it as a whole token, or if it starts with a prefix the source assembles dynamically (82 template-literal sites such as fy-x--${tone}). 263 house-namespace classes are referenced nowhere; three more (is-editor-empty, selectedCell, markedContent, added at runtime by TipTap, prosemirror-tables and pdf.js) were excluded. A rule whose every selector names a dead class can never match: 395 rules, about 1,066 unique lines, 51 KB. A hand check of 21 sampled names (every 13th) found no reference in src or test.

  • fidelity.css: 233 rules, 667 lines. Clusters: the turn-97 storyboard cards (fy-sbcard*, fy-sheethead, fy-boardrail; mixed with live rules such as fy-sbsynopsis in the section from line 1725), the old providers pane (fy-prov__*, 14 names), the turn-102 generate drawer (fy-gendrawer*), 'what Arke made' (fy-made*) and storyboard-row parts that moved to the shot page (fy-swrow__prompt, __ref, __overrides).
  • screens.css: the first-generation scr-* shell; 33 of its 49 scr- classes are dead (sidebar, shellbar, launch, hero, worldcard, prodbar, cutrow, board), 35 rules, 230 lines.
  • season-responsive.css 31 rules, onboarding.css 17, audiobook-look.css 18, audiobook-suggest.css 13, develop-responsive.css 12.
  • A bug-shaped case: system-panel.css defines .fy-system-dot--ready and --busy, but Service (system-panel.tsx:35) renders fy-system-dot ${tone} and no caller passes tone, so every service dot is muted.

Limits: dynamically built names count as live by prefix, so this is a lower bound; classes used only by design-system pages count as dead (they are not product).

Why it matters

Dead rules make the 9,051-line fidelity.css harder to read, mislead anyone searching for a class, and make every live change look riskier than it is; together with CU-02 they are about 5% of the stylesheet every window parses at start.

Options
  1. ADelete cluster by cluster and verify with the layout smoke scriptsRecommended

    One cluster per commit (scr-* shell, storyboard cards, providers pane, generate drawer, made, row parts), each followed by the matching scripts/smoke-*-layout.mjs and class-collision.test.ts. Fix or drop the unused tone prop in system-panel.

  2. BAdd the scan to lint as a ratchet

    Run the same scan in check-client-policy.mjs with an allowlist for third-party classes; the count may only fall. Stops regrowth; pairs well with A.

  3. CStrip unused selectors at build time (PurgeCSS-style)

    Automatic, but leaves the source as it is and is fragile with dynamic class names. Not recommended.

Impact

About 1,066 lines and 51 KB of CSS source (4.6% of lines) from the scan, plus about 120 lines behind dead TSX (CU-02).

Risk

A false positive would be a class name assembled in a way the scan does not see (arrays, data). Each cluster was spot-checked; screenshots from smoke-world-layout, smoke-settings-responsive, smoke-scenes-layout and smoke-productions-layout (Chrome needed) confirm no visual change.

  • packages/client/src/main.tsx:29

Evidence

All 93 client stylesheets (23,092 lines; 1.66 MB source, 1.45 MB without whitespace) are imported from main.tsx and loaded at start; none is imported by a component, deliberately, so the node test runner can import the component graph without a CSS loader (main.tsx:29). Import order is the cascade order, and comments depend on it ('After fidelity.css...', 'Last: Arke's hinge half on a Fold7... stands over the drawers' rules', main.tsx:115). Yet three sheets are imported before the token files (main.tsx:1-3) and two after the render call (main.tsx:163-164), so after the sheet the comment calls last; story-publish.css and arke-half.css both style .fy-page-sheet__body.

fidelity.css is 561 KB (34% of all CSS), has 41 section banners, cites more than 60 design turns and 16 specs, and defines 375 fy- block roots, from the app frame to the bench, editor shell and settings. Its header says every value is a token reference; it has 1,015 raw font sizes.

Styles for one component are spread: .ui-btn has 17 selectors in ui.css and 229 in 35 other sheets; fy-page-sheet is restyled in 26 files, fy-arke in 12, fy-sw__ in 11, fy-ab__ in 8. The seven *-responsive.css files are organised by design turn (168-175), each covering several screens and holding base rules as well as media rules; quiet.css and arke-half.css exist to re-dress rules other sheets own. class-collision.test.ts only checks duplicate bare selectors inside fidelity.css.

Why it matters

Changing a shared class means checking every later sheet that re-dresses it; nobody can tell which file owns a screen's look; dead rules cannot be found by reading; and every window, including a paired phone, parses all of it at start.

Options
  1. ASplit fidelity.css by feature in place, keep one import list, make the order explicitRecommended

    Pure-move fidelity.css's 41 banner sections into feature files imported at the same position, so the cascade is unchanged (the new files, concatenated in import order, must equal today's file byte for byte). Move the three early and two trailing imports to their documented tier and describe the tiers in main.tsx (tokens, primitives, patterns, screens, responsive and re-dress). Extend class-collision.test.ts to all sheets.

  2. BCascade layers through one styles.css index

    @layer tokens, primitives, patterns, screens, redress makes order independent of import position. It changes the winner wherever an earlier, more specific rule now beats a later one, so it needs a full screenshot pass; a good second step after A.

  3. CCSS Modules or component-scoped CSS

    Strongest ownership, but conflicts with the test-runner decision, the re-dress method and 834 querySelector(".…") calls in client tests. Not now.

  4. DLoad CSS per route

    Only possible with lazy routes, which belong to the loading-performance review; it would cut start-up CSS for screens not visited.

Impact

No line change by itself: one 9,051-line file becomes roughly 15-20 files of 200-800 lines, ownership becomes greppable, and CU-03 and CU-10 get easier. A start-up saving only with option D.

Risk

Order-sensitive: a rule that changes position changes the winner at equal specificity, hence the byte-identical concatenation check. Guards: class-collision.test.ts, check-client-policy's block-closure check and the 15 smoke-*-layout scripts (manual; only smoke-editor-effects-preview runs in CI). Check against SPEC-001 R-11 and design turns 168-175, 192, 202 and 227 for intended overrides.

Cited specs

Evidence

npm run lint runs check-client-policy.mjs, check-master.mjs, build-review.mjs --check and build-publish-review.mjs --check before oxlint (package.json:24).

  • check-client-policy.mjs: token files byte-identical to design-system/_ds; a .dark scope and the exact 'Geist Sans' name; every stylesheet closes its blocks and comments; no hex/rgb/hsl/oklch colour outside tokens in CSS or TSX; a light-ramp surface needs a .dark counterpart; toast tokens; the reduced-motion policy; no credential or storage API outside an allowlist.
  • check-master.mjs (design master only): frames from turn 139 set type through tokens, legacy raw sizes ratcheted at 12,513; no bitmap-only cards; anchors resolve; no 'All changes saved' footer from turn 138; a turns.json ledger so a turn or binding rule cannot disappear.
  • build-review.mjs: 612 screens (75 built, 55 drifted, 482 drawn) must resolve to master frames; 172 list control labels that must appear in the frame. The labels are typed into the script, not read from the client.
  • build-publish-review.mjs asserts 22 frames (line 19) but prints '21 frames' (line 43).
  • class-collision.test.ts: duplicate bare selectors inside fidelity.css only.

Nothing checks structure: hand-rolled dialogs and popovers, raw type sizes in the client (the master's turn-139 rule is not applied to the code), dead selectors, breakpoints or components importing screens. The earlier clean-ups regrew: loading.tsx records 'the one loading state' and CSS now has six spinner keyframes; 'every dialog on the body' has exceptions (CU-01).

Why it matters

Ratchets already work in this repository (check-master's legacy count only falls). Without one, each fix in this report is a one-off that the next feature can undo by copying the nearest example.

Options
  1. AOne more rule: a ratchet on hand-rolled overlaysRecommended

    Count bespoke overlay constructs outside the owning modules; the count may fall and may not rise. Today's baseline is 85 matches.

    const OWNERS = new Set(["components/page-sheet.tsx", "components/editor-dialog.tsx", "components/menu.tsx"]);
const BESPOKE = /<dialog\b|role="dialog"|\.showModal\(|(?:document|window)\.addEventListener\("(?:mousedown|pointerdown)"/g;
let n = 0;
for (const p of walk(SRC)) if (p.endsWith(".tsx") && !OWNERS.has(relative(SRC, p).split(sep).join("/"))) n += (read(p).match(BESPOKE) ?? []).length;
if (n > LEGACY_BESPOKE_OVERLAYS) fail("new hand-rolled dialog or popover: use PageSheet, EditorDialog or usePopover", `${n} > ${LEGACY_BESPOKE_OVERLAYS}`);
  2. BA raw-font-size ratchet for client CSS

    Apply the master's turn-139 rule to the code: the 1,440 raw sizes may only fall. Mirrors an existing design rule exactly; addresses CU-10 rather than duplication.

  3. CA dead-class ratchet

    Run the CU-03 scan in lint with an allowlist for third-party classes.

Impact

About 15 lines of script; stops regrowth of the largest duplication class (85 bespoke constructs today). Also fix the '21 frames' message.

Risk

A ratchet blocks a PR that adds a legitimate new surface until it uses a primitive or lowers the count elsewhere, which is the intent. Comments that mention <dialog> count too, as with today's colour rule; accept the noise or strip comments first.

Evidence
  • Spinners and pulses: loading.tsx records 'the one loading state', yet CSS defines six identical to { transform: rotate(360deg) } keyframes (fy-ab-spin, fy-account-spin, fy-ad-spin, fy-bench-spin, fy-comic-spin, fy-launch-spin) and five identical 1 to .35 to 1 pulses (fy-ap-pulse, fy-enh-pulse, fy-note-pulse, fy-pulse, launch-pulse) plus three near copies; TSX uses 32 distinct busy or progress class names.
  • Tabs: ui.tsx Tabs is used only by the unused TabPanels; 13 files hand-roll role="tablist". editor-panel-tabs.tsx has the best keyboard model (arrows, Home/End, roving tabindex); the shared one has none.
  • Switches: ui.tsx Switch is used 5 times in 3 files; 10 raw role="switch" controls in 5 files (settings-providers x4, shell.tsx x3, settings-models, device-notifications, stage-plate), most styled fy-prov__switch.
  • Empty states: EmptyState (layout.tsx:48) is used 55 times in 23 files, but TSX also uses 43 bespoke *empty* classes, and fy-bible__empty (fidelity.css:4866) is borrowed by four other screens as a de-facto shared style.
  • Progress: 7 native <progress> and 7 div role="progressbar", no shared component.
  • Commit-on-blur number and time fields: 8 implementations (NumberField, SecondsField, SecondsStep, EffectNumberField, EffectTimeField, EffectTypedField, TimeField, ClockField); EffectTypedField (editor-effect-fields.tsx:15) is already generic over parse and validate.
Why it matters

Each copy has slightly different keyboard and visual behaviour, and where a shared primitive exists it is often the weakest version, so nobody adopts it.

Options
  1. APromote the best implementation into ui.tsx and adopt it as screens are touchedRecommended

    Tabs with EditorPanelTabs' keyboard model; one fy-spin and one fy-pulse keyframe in globals.css; an inline variant of EmptyState replacing fy-bible__empty; a ProgressBar; a CommitField from EffectTypedField; Switch adopted in Settings.

  2. BDocument the primitives and leave the copies

    Cheap; regrowth continues.

Impact

About 10 keyframe blocks and 60 CSS lines at once; an estimated 300-400 TSX and CSS lines as the 13 tablists, 10 switches and 8 fields adopt shared parts (from sampled sizes).

Risk

Client tests query class names heavily (834 querySelector(".…") calls and about 3,760 fy- mentions), so class renames ripple into tests; keep the old class names on adopters where tests depend on them.

CU-14Breakpoints are unnamed literals with off-by-one boundariesSimplificationUser journeyEffort SLow riskHigh confidence
Where

  • packages/client/src/lib/arke-half.ts:13
  • packages/client/src/screens/editor-responsive.tsx:9

Evidence

CSS has 294 @media blocks with 69 distinct conditions. The working breakpoints are 599/600 and 1099/1100, but max-width: 600px appears 5 times (audiobook-activity.css:38 and four editor-effect-*.css files) and max-width: 1100px 5 times (fidelity.css:1061, 4055, 4669, 4807, 4875), so at exactly 600 or 1100px those rules apply while the JS hooks report the other layout. art-direction.css:13 has a one-pixel (width: 1100px) patch, and off-grid widths include 359, 640, 650, 699, 700, 720, 760, 767, 800, 859, 899, 900, 1199 and 1300px.

In TSX, 131 useMediaQuery calls in 56 files pass literal strings: "(max-width: 599px)" 59 times and "(max-width: 1099px)" 37 times. Only ARKE_HALF_QUERY (lib/arke-half.ts:13) and CUT_PHONE_QUERY (editor-responsive.tsx:9) are named.

Why it matters

A layout boundary is a product decision; as literals it drifts between CSS and JS (it already has at 600 and 1100px), and a reader cannot tell a deliberate 899px from a slip.

Options
  1. AName the queries and fix the boundariesRecommended

    Export PHONE, COMPACT, COARSE and ARKE_HALF plus usePhone() and useCompact() from lib/media-query.ts and replace the 96 literals; change the ten 600/1100 rules to 599/1099 (or the JS to match) once the intended side is confirmed; list the canonical breakpoints in testing.md and flag new non-canonical max-width values in lint.

  2. BPostCSS custom media for CSS

    @custom-media --phone gives CSS one source too, but adds a build plugin; optional later.

Impact

96 string literals replaced by named imports across 56 files; 10 boundary rules corrected; one one-pixel patch removed.

Risk

Windows exactly 600 or 1100px wide change layout; smoke-world-layout includes a 600px window. Check intended widths against design turns 168-175 and 202.

Experience · UJ · 15 findings

User journey I: first run, setup, worldbuilding and navigation

The first-run and worldbuilding journeys are carefully reasoned and well guarded wherever money is spent or something is destroyed, but they have accumulated parallel paths, stale screens and a few outright dead ends. Two are plain bugs: Edit the sheet on a location or faction addresses a route that does not exist and drops the person on the world picker, and factions have no visible New control at desktop widths. The no-AI path promised by Start lightweight breaks at the first hand-made character, because a typed sentence is staged as a brief that cannot be accepted until an agent drafts it. After first run the guided setup cannot be re-entered and the writing model is pinned on 18 separate agents, so the most common configuration change is the hardest one; most other wins are small (one creation pattern and one vocabulary for sibling entities, one progress renderer, a launch screen without inert sign-in affordances, and a Home that resumes where the person actually was).

How this area is built, and how it was reviewed

The entry experience is client-led. App.tsx defines nine top-level routes outside worlds and productions: the launch surface (/ and /starting), the setup wizard (/setup), the founding build's watch screen (/building/:worldId), Home (/worlds), New world (/worlds/new), Publications, an orphaned /first-run and the retired /activity redirect. Settings is not a page: every /settings/* address renders as a sheet over the last remembered screen (SPEC-042 R-5, R-6), with 12 rail panes, a hidden Downloads pane and six retired addresses redirected.

Every start opens on the launch surface; after Continue it goes to /building if a build is running, to /setup until onboarding is done, otherwise to /worlds (launch.tsx:267-275). Onboarding is a 12-state wizard with guided, advanced and lightweight personas, persisted by the coordinator (SPEC-016 R-21 – R-28). A world is created either from a form (legacy createWorld plus client-side seeding) or from a founding conversation whose blueprint is reviewed in cards and founded by one priced build (SPEC-031).

Inside a world, WorldLayout draws one chrome bar (its back button is always Worlds) and a sticky row of nine pills; the Cast pill fronts four ledgers (characters, locations, factions, props) through a chip row. One SheetDetail component renders characters, locations and factions, with character-only sub-pages (Reference, More looks, Voice, main photo, model sheet) and a location Reference page. Hand-made sheets are staged as proposals and drafted by an agent before acceptance (#1916); canon entries and props are created directly. Overlays (Activity, System, Studio assistant, contextual chat, account menu, pairing and update dialogs) sit over every screen. Phones and the Fold share the routes; layouts change below 1100px and 600px, and remote sessions replace host-only controls with on your PC notes.

Scope and method

Static reading of the client route table (App.tsx), launch.tsx, onboarding.tsx, shell.tsx (first run, world picker, new world and founding conversation, Settings layout, General, Harness, Sign-in, Sample world), building.tsx, world.tsx (layout, overview, ledgers, sheet detail, new sheet, canon, edit), proposals.tsx, character-reference.tsx, character-voice.tsx, props.tsx, settings-providers.tsx, settings-remote-access.tsx, remote-entry.tsx, pairing-prompt.tsx, chrome.tsx, studio-assistant.tsx, update-announcement.tsx and the CSS that decides visibility (cast.css, fidelity.css). Coordinator code was read only where it shapes what the person sees: save-onboarding, create-world, create-sheet-from-sentence, the sheet-seed gate rule, onboarding's agent writes in app-settings.ts, world scan ordering and the start-up environment check.

Journeys were built from route definitions, navigate( calls, button conditions and on-screen strings, each step cited as path:line. Tests and smoke scripts were read to see what is guarded, and git log was used read-only to date two regressions. Nothing was run: no build, app launch, browser rendering or test execution, so CSS-dependent visibility and timing claims carry their stated confidence. The private specifications were not available; SPEC ids are taken from code comments and marked check against.

Not covered (other reviewers): productions under /w/:id/p/…, publications, production chat, runtime and world-open performance, the contents of the Activity and System panels, and component/CSS structure beyond what changes a flow.

UJ-01Edit the sheet on a location or faction lands on the world pickerUser journeySimplificationEffort SLow riskHigh confidence
Where
  • packages/client/src/screens/world.tsx:2176-2187
  • packages/client/src/App.tsx:310
  • packages/client/src/App.tsx:317-325

  • packages/client/src/screens/world.tsx:2340-2398
Evidence

SheetDetail draws one shared main block for characters, locations and factions (world.tsx:2152-2240, used by both returns at 2356-2398). Its first action, Edit the sheet, navigates to the kind's plural folder:

navigate(
  `/w/${worldId}/${sheet.type === "character" ? "cast" : `${sheet.type}s`}/${sheet.id}/edit`,
)

App.tsx registers only cast/:sheetId/edit (line 310). There is no locations/:sheetId/edit or factions/:sheetId/edit, and the /w/:worldId subtree has no catch-all, so the address falls to the top-level * route, which replaces it with /worlds (App.tsx:393). git log -S shows the cast route is the only edit route that has ever existed (since 77858094f). The edit screen is already kind-aware: editsRole = sheet?.type === "character" (world.tsx:2434) and the written-voice section is added only for characters (2425). Tests mount only cast/maren-kest/edit (sheet-inline-decisions.test.tsx:148, world-layout-frames.test.tsx:66).

Why it matters

Editing a place or a faction by hand is the core of the add-and-refine loop for anything that is not a character. The press leaves the world with no message and lands on Home; the only other way to change the prose is to ask World Chat. To someone mid-thought it looks like the app lost their place, or their work.

Options
  1. ARoute the existing edit screen for every sheet kindRecommended

    Add locations/:sheetId/edit and factions/:sheetId/edit beside the cast route, rendering the same component (rename CharacterEditScreen to SheetEditScreen). Add location-edit and faction-edit to the screen registry so the SPEC-001 R-7 navigation walk mounts them, and a test that presses Edit on each kind. WorldLayout already treats any /edit path as a fixed frame (world.tsx:249-252). Two lines of routing plus tests.

  2. BBuild every sheet address from one helper

    Introduce sheetPath(kind, id, page) generated from the same table as the routes and use it for every navigate to a sheet, so an unrouted sub-page cannot be addressed. Larger, and best done with UJ-10's kind table.

  3. CCatch unknown addresses inside the world

    Add a * child under /w/:worldId that lands on the world's Overview with a short notice rather than leaving the world. Defence in depth for future slips; does not restore editing.

Impact

Restores hand editing for 2 of the 3 sheet kinds that show an Edit button and removes an unexpected exit (one extra navigation plus a world reopen) on every attempt. Estimated from the route table: 2 missing routes behind 1 shared button.

Risk

Character-only parts of the edit screen are already gated by type. Guard with client test/routes.test.tsx, the registry navigation test (SPEC-001 R-7) and test/sheet-inline-decisions.test.tsx; check the edit form against the location and faction sheet shapes.

Evidence

When the harness is not healthy the New sheet button reads Create as sketch (world.tsx:2858) and the location form says without the harness running, the sentence seeds the sheet as-is — still a sketch through the gate (world.tsx:3028). The coordinator stages the sentence with requiresDraft: this.authoring !== null (coordinator.ts:10199); the authoring service exists whenever an adapter is composed, ready or not, so a sheetSeed is recorded (authoring.ts:252). With no ready adapter no draft runs (10227-10253). The gate then refuses the unchanged brief: This is still the saved brief. Draft the sheet or edit its prose before accepting. (sheet-seed.ts:20), the pending card says not drafted · your brief is saved — open it to draft the sheet (world.tsx:1003-1004), and the review's Accept is disabled with Draft the sheet before accepting. (connected.tsx:57). The same screen shows DegradedBanner: this screen's actions are disabled until OpenCode is back (layout.tsx:100-101) while Create as sketch stays enabled. Lightweight setup promises Create worlds, edit by form and write your stories (onboarding.tsx:236). The brief rule is deliberate (#1916; coordinator test sheets.test.ts:361 and client sheet-inline-decisions.test.tsx:527-547).

Why it matters

A lightweight user, or anyone whose writing agent is down, types a character and gets a card that cannot be accepted and a button that sends them to a drafter they do not have. The copy on three surfaces promises the opposite. With an agent, the person also approves a draft of their own sentence, which is the gate working as intended because an agent wrote it.

Options
  1. AWithout a drafter, stage the sentence as the sketchRecommended

    When no drafting run can start (adapter not ready, or no writing model), stage without sheetSeed and settle it as Begin does, so Create as sketch lands a sketch in one press. Keep the brief rule whenever an agent will draft. Check against #1916 and the sheet acceptance requirements before changing the gate.

  2. BAdd 'Use my sentence' to the review

    Keep the coordinator rule; give the review panel a one-press action that writes the brief into the first section as prose and accepts. Honest about the extra step, no gate change.

  3. CCopy only

    Rename the button Save brief, drop the 'seeds the sheet as-is' line and make the banner say drafting is needed. Truthful, but the no-AI path stays a dead end.

Impact

Without a writing agent: from a dead end to 2 presses per character, place or faction (type, Create as sketch). With an agent: unchanged. Affects every lightweight install and any session whose harness is down.

Risk

Touches the acceptance gate. Guard with coordinator test/sheets/sheets.test.ts ('attended sentence seeds'), test/harness/model-routing.test.ts and client test/sheet-inline-decisions.test.tsx ('undrafted briefs (#1916)'); check against SPEC-016 R-21 – R-28 for the lightweight promise.

Evidence

Onboarding is the only guided way to connect a writing account and check a model. Once its plan is done, /setup redirects to /worlds (onboarding.tsx:247, #2339), and General's Studio setup row switches from Set up an AI writing agent & tools to Manage AI models & tools, which opens AI models (shell.tsx:2456). The empty Home tells a lightweight user Add AI whenever you need it with a Settings button to General (shell.tsx:482); the phone index summarises AI models as images, video, voice, music with no mention of writing (shell.tsx:1663).

On finish, onboarding writes the chosen model into every non-operational agent that has none:

if (writingModel) for (const member of ROSTER) {
  if (!member.operationalOnly && !["stage-designer", "chapter-visual-reviewer"].includes(member.name) && !agents[member.name]?.model) {
    agents[member.name] = { ...agents[member.name], model: writingModel };
  }
}

That pins 18 of the 22 roster agents (coordinator test/setup/onboarding.test.ts:32-40 expects it), although a role without a model already inherits Story writer's (roster.ts:466-472, issue 2419). Afterwards the only control is Settings › Harness › Advanced · which model runs each writing agent (shell.tsx:2257), a list of every agent with a select whose empty option reads Ask the harness (agents.tsx:82). Credentials are split between Providers (keys, rail 1) and Sign-in (vendor accounts, rail 9), and the Codex image sign-in asks for a terminal command, codex login (settings-providers.tsx:229).

Why it matters

Switching the writing model, or adding AI after starting lightweight, is the most common configuration change after first run. Today it means up to 18 selects behind an Advanced toggle, or an unguided walk across Sign-in, Providers, AI models and Harness, while the friendly flow that already does it is locked away.

Options
  1. AMake guided setup re-enterableRecommended

    Allow /setup after done, opening at the writing step with current choices loaded, and point Home's Add AI button and General's Studio setup row there. Must keep #2339: a stale address never restarts or overwrites a completed plan; re-entry edits it explicitly.

  2. BOne writing-model control, inherited by the roles

    Onboarding sets only Story writer; the other roles inherit (issue 2419). Add one Writing model row on General that sets Story writer and says how many roles override it, with a reset. The per-agent list stays under Advanced for people who want it. Pairs well with A.

  3. COne place for credentials

    Fold Sign-in's vendor rows into Providers (a service shows key or account sign-in), and offer an in-app sign-in where the harness supports it instead of a terminal command. Rail drops from 12 to 11 panes.

Impact

Writing-model switch: from 2 navigations plus up to 18 selects to 2 navigations plus 1 select (B). Adding AI after lightweight: from 5 or more navigations across 3–4 panes to the existing 4–5 press guided flow (A). Counted from the traced steps in journeys J6 and J8.

Risk

Check against SPEC-016 R-21 – R-28 (journey progress, not a settings authority), SPEC-034 R-14/R-16 (General is defaults, not routing) and SPEC-042 R-1/R-4 (AI models owns the switch and the credential remedy). A capability row renders the same projection — transferProgress — rather than computing its own* (settings-downloads.tsx:15-27). transferProgress is used by Downloads, engine panes and local models. The launch surface computes its own percent, active component and time left (launch.tsx:225-262) and its own retry buttons (387-408); onboarding's progress step renders raw bytesDone/bytesTotal bars with its own pause, resume and retry (onboarding.tsx:219-232). A returning user mid-download sees the launch band; a first-run user sees the onboarding step; both also link to Downloads.

Why it matters

Three renderings of one set of transfers can disagree, and the rule written to prevent exactly that is bypassed on the two screens a new person sees first.

Options
  1. AOne progress list from the shared projectionRecommended

    Extract a SetupProgressList driven by transferProgress and use it on launch, onboarding and Downloads; keep each surface's framing.

  2. BDrop onboarding's progress step

    After Set up and start, go to Home and let the launch-style band or Downloads show progress. Fewer screens; pairs with UJ-06 A.

  3. CLeave as is

    Each surface reads the same component states; drift is possible but not observed.

Impact

2 independent progress computations removed; figures agree on all 3 surfaces; about 60 lines of duplicated progress UI collapse.

Risk

Check against SPEC-033 R-82 and SPEC-016 R-1 (actual transfer progress, commit e43e1e6e9). Guard with client test/launch-lifecycle.test.tsx, test/onboarding.test.tsx, the Downloads tests and scripts/smoke-launch-layout.mjs.

Pairing is a one-off but it is the phone's first impression: a code that appears only after a second press further down the pane, typed on a phone keyboard within five minutes. The owner approval, single-use code and Tailscale-only transport are right and should stay.

    When the QR is drawn, request a pairing code at once and show it beside the QR (refresh on expiry). One press fewer, and the instruction no longer points down the page.

  2. BPrefill the code from the QR

    When the device check succeeds, go straight to the studio as the first approval already does. Check against design turn 158i.

Impact

PC: 5 presses to 4 (A). Phone: 8 typed characters to none (B). Every later phone visit: 1 press fewer (C).

Risk

A and C are presentation; B changes the pairing protocol. Guard with coordinator and desktop test/remote-access.test.ts, client test/remote-pairing.test.tsx, test/remote-access.test.tsx and apps/desktop/scripts/smoke-remote-access.mjs.

Experience · UP · 12 findings

User journey II: productions (writing, audiobook, video, comics, audio drama, interactive, music) and publishing

Productions are rich and carefully guarded (prices before spend, the accept gate, checks before export), but the journey changes shape with every kind, and its last step, publishing, is the least consistent part of the product. The same Arke Player package is made through four different client sheets and only one of them offers Submit; Export lives on seven screens under five labels, and the button called Other exports opens a different sheet depending on where it is pressed. Navigation has drifted: duplicate and retired addresses, Overview meaning three different screens, desktop and phone page lists that disagree (Story structure cannot be reached on desktop), a film door whose second step has been unreachable since 8 September, and five ways to start generating a clip, three of which leave the production. The best single move is a per-production Publish page built from components that already exist, followed by one Arke Player sheet and one navigation definition; the clearest performance fix in this slice is the rail's audiobook count, which makes the coordinator prepare the whole book again after every manuscript autosave.

How this area is built, and how it was reviewed

Every production lives under /w/:worldId/p/:prodId, wrapped by ProductionLayout in production-shell.tsx, which draws a left rail on desktop and a page strip on phones. productionShape (contracts production-shape.ts) maps three media (story, video, music) and 13 creatable kinds onto five rail variants: episodic video (Overview, Episodes tree, Takes, Artifacts, Generate, Cut), music (Tracks, Artifacts), audio drama (Episodes, Adaptation, Cast, Artifacts), story (Dashboard, Cast, Develop, Overview, Chapters, then Audiobook or Pages, Artifacts) and other video, including interactive movies and visual novels (Dashboard, Cast, Develop, Overview, Scenes, Branch map, Artifacts, Generate, Cut). The index address dispatches to six different home screens.

Creation starts at four doors on /productions/new. Make a film jumps straight into a conversational setup (/productions/setup/:setupId, Review production then Create production); an adapted audio drama and a graphic novel reach the same setup through Plan with Arke; the other kinds are created from a short form.

Writing happens in the chapter workspace (views Chapter, Manuscript, Audiobook, Audio Studio). Video work happens in the scene workspace, the shot page, Generate (Takes, bench and contact-sheet lenses) and the Cut; comics in Pages; audio drama in episode scripts and their Audio Studio. Generation either prices on the press or asks in a sheet, and results arrive as takes, blocks or pages that are accepted through the gate.

Delivery differs per kind: a shared five-step Publish sheet (EPUB, PDF, M4B) plus two different Other exports sheets for books, Export film in the Cut, Export on Pages, Tracks and the Branch Map, and Publish… for audio drama. Arke Player packages come from one coordinator function through four client sheets. Creator submission to Arke Player (the AONIK service) appears beside one of those sheets' results and on the app-level Publications page.

Scope and method

Static reading at HEAD 42d3def (0.5.116). Client: routes in App.tsx; production-shell.tsx (desktop rail, switcher, Develop screen) and lib/production-navigation.ts (phone page strip); every production home (production-dashboard.tsx, development.tsx, drama-episodes.tsx, music-album.tsx, comic-dashboard.tsx); creation (world.tsx door and step two, production-setup.tsx); chapter tree and chapter workspace views, chapter and manuscript review controls; the audiobook show page; every publish and export surface (story-publish.tsx, audiobook-export.tsx, arke-player-export.tsx, story-export.tsx, the comic, music and audio drama sheets, editor-export.tsx, publication-export.tsx, creator-publishing.tsx, publications.tsx); Generate, Takes and bench entry points and the scene workspace generation presses; spend and price-confirmation surfaces.

Coordinator productions/ was read only where a step's effect needed confirming (the exportArkePlayer dispatch, the audiobook door, setup defaults, web-package listing). Journeys were built from route definitions, rail item definitions, navigate( and Link calls, button labels and the conditions that show or disable them; each step cites path:line. Git history was read, without changing anything, to date the Watch-door change (commit c890258b2) and the removal of Story structure from the desktop rail (commit d1eacb907) and its return on phones (commit e3a8aa591).

Not covered: first run and worldbuilding (another reviewer), the Cut editor's internals, the chapter audiobook block editor and Audio Studio beyond their entry points, coordinator correctness, and anything that needs the app running. The private specifications were not available; SPEC and design-turn citations are named so they can be checked, never interpreted. Nothing in the repository was changed.

Evidence

Verified in code:

  • Labels: Publish on Chapters and on the Audiobook page, Publish… on the audio drama home, Export on Pages, Tracks and the Branch Map, Export… in a chapter's Audiobook view, Export film in the Cut. Five labels on seven screens.
  • The shared Publish sheet (five steps: Edition, Chapters, Formatting & style, Preview, Files) has a ghost button Other exports. From Chapters it opens Export manuscript (Word or EPUB); from the Audiobook page it opens Export audiobook (player.html, chapter MP3s, MP4 video, Arke Player).
  • A book's Arke Player package is reached only as Audiobook, Publish, Other exports, Arke Player, then Make package. It cannot be reached from Chapters or the dashboard, so a text-only book has to go through the Audiobook page to package its EPUB for the Player.
  • An EPUB can be made three ways: the Publish sheet (style review, captured immutable edition), Export manuscript (two presses), and inside the Arke Player package (the book, EPUB).
  • Made outputs are listed in five places: the Publish sheet's private editions and /publications; Export manuscript's last four Delivered rows; the audio drama home's Editions; Export film's rows and Publications' jobs; Publications' Web packages. A comic's CBZ, PDF and EPUB appear only in the dialog's done rows.
  • /publications is an app-level page opened from Home's Open publication (shell.tsx:358). Nothing inside a production links to it except the status line after a submission.
  • The retired exports address redirects to cut?export=1 for every kind, including books and comics.
Why it matters

Publishing is where a creator decides the work is finished. Today the place, the word and the next sheet change with the kind of production, and two identically named buttons lead to different sheets, so the pattern cannot be learned once. The same readiness and blocker logic is also written several times, and help and support instructions have to be written per kind.

Options
  1. AAdd one Publish page per production, built from existing componentsRecommended

    New address /w/:worldId/p/:prodId/publish with a rail item in the same place for every kind. Top: the outputs this kind supports as cards with readiness, using the Branch Map's pattern (blocked · N, with Go to), each opening the existing sheet. Below: this production's made outputs, using the existing lists filtered by production (StoryEditionLibrary and PublicationJobs already accept productionId; WebPackages, drama editions and comic files need a filter). Keep in-context buttons as shortcuts to the same sheets. Trade-off: one more rail item; needs agreement on the address because exports is retired to the Cut.

  2. BKeep per-kind buttons but standardise label, slot and Other exports

    Use one label (Publish) in the same header slot on each kind's main working screen; rename Other exports to name its destination (for example Word or EPUB file, Audiobook files and Arke Player); add Arke Player to the Publish sheet opened from Chapters. Cheaper, but outputs stay listed in five places.

  3. CFold everything into the app-level Publications page with a production filter

    Least new UI, but the person still leaves the production to publish, and Publications already mixes four unrelated kinds of output.

Impact

Reaching a book's Arke Player options: 3 presses on the Audiobook page and 4 from any other book page today (Audiobook, Publish, Other exports, Arke Player); 2 from any book page with option A (Publish, Arke Player). Export labels 5 to 1. Places that list a production's outputs 5 to 1 (plus the app-level Publications). Counted from the code paths cited.

Risk

SPEC-039 R-1 and T-5 retired exports into the Cut, so use a new address rather than reviving it. Label and structure tests: client audiobook-export.test.tsx, exports.test.tsx, story-download.test.tsx, story-pdf.test.tsx, productions-layout.test.tsx, development.test.tsx, drama-adaptation.test.tsx, plus the publish smoke scripts. Check against SPEC-058 R-1 to R-8, design turn 224 (the shared Publish sheet), SPEC-057 R-71 to R-76 and SPEC-064 R-50.

Evidence

Verified in code; cost not measured:

  • The rail calls useAudiobookDoorAsk(..., isStory) for every production with chapters, which includes graphic novels. For a graphic novel the rail shows Pages, not the audiobook count, so every answer it asks for is unused.
  • The ask's stamp includes each chapter's version and body hash, so every manuscript save changes it. The chapter workspace autosaves after 1.2 s idle. Only the rail and the Audiobook page ask; on Chapters, a chapter or Cast the rail alone drives it.
  • The coordinator answers open-audiobook with audiobookDoor, which calls prepareBook: every chapter prepared as its press would prepare it, with counts, readers and price.
  • The rail also measures the cut on every render: editorTimeline (which seeds and migrates a first picture timeline when none is saved), deriveCut or resolvePictureTimeline, and buildRenderPlan for media-only productions. None is memoised.
  • ProductionLayout re-renders on every store change because useOpenWorldGuard reads the whole store through useStore(), so this runs on every store update, and coordinator events such as job progress update the store.
Why it matters

While someone writes, the coordinator keeps re-preparing and re-pricing the whole book for a number nobody is looking at, competing with the work they are doing. Client renders repeat timeline work on every frame. The 2026-09-13 refactor record (docs/issues/101) found the same buildRenderPlan-in-render pattern in the Cut and fixed it with useMemo; the rail was not covered.

Options
  1. AAsk less, and memoise the rail's figuresRecommended

    Pass isStory && !shape.hasPages to the rail's ask. Drop body hash from the rail's stamp (ask on chapter add, remove or status change, or show the count from the last door the Audiobook page fetched). Memoise the cut figures on the production, timeline and artifacts identities, and subscribe the layout to the world slice and connection rather than the whole store. Small, local changes.

  2. BAdd a cheap read-count query to the coordinator

    A query that counts chapters read from the audiobook records without block planning or pricing; the rail uses it and the Audiobook page keeps the full door. More work, but keeps the count exact.

  3. CDrop the Audiobook and Cut counts from the rail

    Design turn 192 already hides counts of none; removing these two removes the work. A product decision, since SPEC-047 R-29 asks for the read count.

Impact

Graphic novels: 100% of rail door asks removed. Books: with a save every 10 to 60 s, about 60 to 360 whole-book preparations an hour that nobody looks at would stop (from the autosave interval and the one-in-flight coalescing in openAudiobook; a 23-chapter book such as the Undersong release prepares 23 chapters each time). Rail render work moves from every store frame to production changes. Measure with the React Profiler and coordinator timings before and after.

Risk

The rail's count must match the Audiobook page (SPEC-047 R-29, turn 146) and the Cut figure must match the Cut header (issue 508). Tests: client audiobook-door.test.tsx, audiobook-show.test.tsx, development.test.tsx, cut-layout.test.tsx. Overlaps the client state and loading reviewer's subscription findings; coordinate rather than fix twice.

    Remove the dead video branch and its tests and correct both door texts. Keeps today's behaviour; leaves three patterns.

  3. CMake every door conversation-first

    Send every door to the setup and choose the kind there. Consistent, but slower for people who already know what they want and need no conversation.

A film today takes a door choice, a conversation, the Format select, Review and Create (4 decisions plus a conversation) before anything exists; with option A, Start empty takes 3 decisions and the conversation becomes optional. Option B alone removes about 140 lines of unreachable code and tests.

Tooling · BT · 15 findings

Build, typecheck, lint, tests, CI and the contributor's workflow (measured)

The repository's CI is capacity-bound, not test-bound: in the week to 2026-11-07 it ran 744 CI workflows (8,966 jobs, 60,299 runner-minutes, two thirds on Windows) against a ceiling of 20 concurrently running jobs, so jobs waited a median 18 minutes and a p90 of 3.5 hours before starting. CI is also not acting as a gate: 287 of the 303 pull requests merged that week (95%) were merged a median 3 minutes after their CI run started, long before it finished, and 88% of pushes to main are cancelled before they finish (23 of 303 verified green), so a breakage fans out into dozens of failing agent pull requests — 180 failed runs (45% of all CI minutes) shared a failure signature with five or more neighbours. Inside each run, the typecheck gate builds 11 separate TypeScript programs that each re-check the same 76k-line contracts source; a single combined Node program checks the same files in 137 s instead of 483 s, one test expression costs 17% of the coordinator check, and the three largest programs do not fit in the 2 GB heap Node defaults to on machines with less than 16 GB. The client ships one 5.86 MB entry chunk (9.4x the 626 kB flagged on 2026-08-04, never acted on), 20 client test files idle 7-20 s after their last assertion, and the contributor guides have grown into 58k words of prepended notes. The deliberate design (Windows and Linux on every push, the silence guard, the separate film job, discovery-based sharding, the hand-formatted house style) holds up and should be kept; the recommended changes make it cheaper rather than smaller.

How this area is built, and how it was reviewed

The repository is an npm-workspaces monorepo of ten packages and one Electron app. Every internal package publishes its TypeScript source ("types": "./src/index.ts"), so each workspace's tsc --noEmit compiles its dependencies' source too; npm run typecheck runs 11 such programs one after another. npm run build runs each workspace's build: the client (Vite 7, one entry chunk), the engine (esbuild plus dts-bundle-generator over coordinator source) and the desktop main bundle, whose build script rebuilds the client. npm run lint is eight custom Node checks (design-system parity, client token policy, private-docs hygiene) followed by oxlint packages apps; it takes 3.5 s. Tests use node --test with the tsx loader, one process per file, 1,188 test files.

CI (ci.yml) runs on every pull request and every push to main: one Ubuntu job for lint, typecheck, build and the CI-planner test; coordinator tests in eight shards on each of ubuntu-latest and windows-latest (Node's --test-shard, which splits the discovered file list by index); an other-workspaces job per OS; and the Production Chat film per OS, 21 jobs in all, each running its own npm ci (12 s Linux, 24 s Windows median). scripts/ci-test.mjs relays output and kills a step after ten silent minutes under a 30-minute job ceiling. effects.yml and engine.yml add two jobs each on every push to main and on matching pull requests. A green run costs a median 152 runner-minutes (102 Windows) and 22 minutes of wall clock once it has runners; the critical path is the Windows other-workspaces job (14 minutes, the client suite alone 10).

Contributors are mostly agent sessions (304 claude/ and codex/ PR branches in the week), told by CLAUDE.md to branch, push and request review; there are no required checks, 95% of pull requests merge before their CI run finishes, and pushes to main cancel any in-progress main run.

Scope and method

Examined: root and workspace package.json scripts, every tsconfig, tsconfig.base.json, .oxlintrc.json, the nine-step lint pipeline, scripts/ (79 files, 35 root smoke scripts plus 15 in apps/desktop/scripts), design-system check scripts, all five workflows and both composite actions, the test suites, and CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, docs/development/README.md, testing.md, code-map.md and maintenance.md. Earlier audits checked: docs/code-analysis/2026-08-04-startup-logic.html and 2026-09-05-documentation-audit.md.

Method:

  • Local measurements in this Linux container (Firecracker VM, nproc 4, free -m 16,086 MB, Node 22.23.4, npm 10.9.9, TypeScript 5.9.3). Other reviewers ran workloads at the same time (load average 1-9), so local wall times are upper bounds; each command, its wall time and peak RSS (via a Python getrusage wrapper, since GNU time is absent) are listed under measurements.
  • CI facts from the GitHub API, read-only: every CI run created 2026-10-31 to 2026-11-07 (744 runs) with job and step timings, full logs of one green main run (42343860689) parsed per test suite, the checks-job log of run 42386846699, failed-step logs of three failing runs, and the 303 pull requests merged that week (REST pulls API) matched to their CI runs.
  • Experiments that change no tracked file: a combined tsconfig placed in the scratch folder, exclusion runs, --generateTrace for contracts, coordinator and client, TypeScript 7.0.2 installed into the scratch folder, sourcemap attribution of the client bundle, an esbuild bundle of coordinator.ts to compare import costs, and a probe of all 338 client test files for time between last result and process exit.

Not covered: whole-suite local test runs (minutes to hours; CI logs used instead), Windows-runner profiling, the packaging and release workflows beyond reading them, the Electron app itself. Specification content is not in this container; no SPEC requirement was inferred. npm ci was the only command that wrote into the repository (node_modules); git status --short --ignored showed nothing else at the end.

Findings

BT-01CI is capacity-bound: 21-job runs against a 20-job ceiling leave pushes queued for hoursPerformanceUser journeyEffort MLow riskHigh confidence
Where
  • .github/workflows/ci.yml:62
  • .github/workflows/ci.yml:105
  • .github/workflows/ci.yml:132
  • scripts/ci-test-plan.mjs:2
  • scripts/ci-test.mjs:218
Evidence

Week of 2026-10-31 to 2026-11-07, GitHub API (read-only):

  • 744 CI runs, 8,966 jobs that got a runner, 60,299 runner-minutes (Windows 39,788, Linux 20,511). effects.yml and engine.yml ran 314 times each on top.
  • Running jobs plateau at 20 at a time (one 39-job instant coincides with a mass cancellation and looks like an accounting artifact); 18 or more were running for 40.3 hours of the week. A single CI run is 21 jobs, so it cannot start all at once even on an idle account.
  • Queue from job creation to start: median 17.8 min, p75 124.6, p90 210.7, max 282. Run 42364835722 was created at 10:38 and its lint job started at 13:27.
  • A green run (median of 40) is 152 runner-minutes, 102 of them Windows, and 22.0 minutes of wall clock once runners are free. Job time outside the Test step is ~0.6 min on Linux and ~1.1 min on Windows (checkout 11-14 s, Defender 5 s, setup-node 6-21 s, npm ci 19-41 s), about 17 runner-minutes per run.
  • Linux coordinator shards are short: Test-step medians 2.5-4.1 min, jobs 3.0-4.7 min, so setup is ~20% of each. The critical path is Windows: other-workspaces 14.0 min median, Windows shards 8.7-12.6 min.
  • Of the last month's 642 first-parent commits on main, 159 (25%) touched only packages/client plus docs or design-system; 2 were docs-only. Three coordinator tests read client files (test/activity/activity.test.ts:622, test/first-run/first-run.test.ts:173, test/remote-access.test.ts:210).
Why it matters

Every push competes for the same 20 slots, so feedback latency is dominated by waiting, not by test time: results arrive anywhere from ~40 minutes to 4 hours after a push (job queue median 18 minutes, p90 3.5 hours, plus ~22 minutes of running). It is also why merges do not wait for CI (BT-02). Any runner-minute removed from a run is removed from that queue, so savings here compound across ~100 runs a day.

Options
  1. AFewer, fuller jobs per run without dropping coverageRecommended

    Run the Linux coordinator suite in 4 shards instead of 8 (pairs of today's 3-4 minute shards stay well under the 14-minute Windows path), keep 8 on Windows, and apply BT-03, BT-05 and BT-06 to the other jobs. Needs matrix.include for per-OS shard counts and an update to ci-test-plan.test.mjs's matrix assertion. Result: 17 jobs and roughly 135 runner-minutes per green run, so a run fits under the ceiling.

  2. BPath-gate the 16 coordinator shard jobs on pull requests

    Skip the coordinator shards when a PR changes nothing under packages/ other than packages/client (and none of the three client files coordinator tests read), fixtures/, scripts/ci-*, .github/ or package-lock.json; always run everything on main. This copies the policy effects.yml and engine.yml already document (a miss surfaces on main at the next merge). About a quarter of PRs would save ~110 runner-minutes each.

  3. CBuy capacity

    A paid plan raises the concurrent-job ceiling and larger or self-hosted runners shorten jobs. This costs money and leaves the waste in BT-02 untouched; worth revisiting only after A, B and BT-02.

  4. DMerge queue with required checks

    Batching merges (one run per batch instead of PR plus main) needs the repository under an organization for GitHub's merge queue. Largest process change; strongest guarantee.

Impact

A: ~17 runner-minutes and 4 concurrent slots per run (estimate from job-minus-step overheads and the BT-03/05/06 savings). B: ~8,500 runner-minutes a week (316 completed PR runs x 25% x ~108; up to ~11,800 if cancelled runs are counted at full length). With BT-02, weekly demand could fall from ~60,000 to roughly 25,000-35,000 runner-minutes, which on the observed load curve should remove most queueing above an hour.

Risk

Windows and Linux both keep running every test (invariant). Fewer Linux shards raise a Linux job to ~6-9 min, still far from the 30-minute ceiling and the ten-minute silence guard (longest observed silence 19 s on Linux). Path gating can let a client-only change break a coordinator test until main runs; guarded by running everything on main and by ci-test-plan.test.mjs if the filter list is held to the workspace list.

BT-02CI does not gate merges: 95% of pull requests merge minutes after their run starts, and each breakage cascadesUser journeyPerformanceEffort SMedium riskHigh confidence
Where
  • .github/workflows/ci.yml:17
  • .github/workflows/ci.yml:62
  • .github/workflows/effects.yml:25
  • .github/workflows/engine.yml:21
  • CLAUDE.md:341
  • package.json:24
Evidence
  • Of the 303 pull requests merged from 2026-10-31 to 2026-11-07, 287 (95%) were merged before the last CI run on their branch had finished, a median 3.1 minutes after it started; 14 merged after a green run and 1 after a red or cancelled one. There are no required checks (CLAUDE.md:341-351 asks sessions to poll CI before merging).
  • Example: PR #2592 was opened at 06:27:56 on 11-07, its CI run 42347126001 started at 06:27:59, and it was merged at 06:30:11. The run finished at 06:42 with coordinator shards 6/8 and 7/8 failing on both platforms (test/productions/planning.test.ts and test/productions/manuscript.test.ts). The next 57 PR runs, over four hours, failed exactly those four jobs.
  • 255 failed CI runs used 38,114 runner-minutes, 63% of the week. 180 of them (27,057 runner-minutes, 45% of all CI minutes) failed with the same set of failing jobs as at least five other runs within six hours; the other large clusters were 49 runs on 11-04 (shard 1/8 plus other-workspaces) and 44 runs on 11-01/02 failing two client tests on both platforms (test/audiobook-motion.test.tsx, test/recovery-history.test.tsx).
  • Main does not catch it either: cancel-in-progress: true also applies to pushes (ci.yml:17-20), so 267 of 303 push runs were cancelled (on average 11.6 runner-minutes each, mostly while queued), 23 went green and 13 failed; effects.yml and engine.yml cancelled 255 and 217 of their 305 push runs.
  • 39 failed runs included a lint failure, 20 of them lint only (5,387 runner-minutes); lint takes 3.5 s, but the other 20 jobs still run to the end. A sampled one: client policy: hard-coded colours outside the token files (R-11) screens/fidelity.css.
  • All 304 PR branches that week were claude/* (191) or codex/* (113).
Why it matters

The gate spends ~150 runner-minutes on every push but its answer arrives after the merge, so broken code reaches main unverified, main's own runs are cancelled, and every later session inherits the failure and pays to rediscover it. Nearly half of CI capacity goes to these repeats, which is a large part of why the queue is hours long (BT-01).

Options
  1. AMake CI a merge gate: required checks plus auto-mergeRecommended

    Add a ruleset on main requiring the CI jobs (simplest: one small aggregating job with needs: on all others and if: always(), so a future path filter cannot leave a required check pending) and merge with gh pr merge --auto (without --delete-branch, per CLAUDE.md). Merges then wait for a green run; CLAUDE.md's existing instruction to poll before merging becomes enforced instead of advisory. Merge latency becomes CI wall time plus queue, so land BT-01's savings first or together.

  2. BLet main runs finish

    cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }} verifies main continuously in batches. At today's ~43 merges a day it could add roughly 20,000-35,000 runner-minutes a week (25-35 completed main runs a day at ~176 runner-minutes including effects and engine, less today's ~8,500), so prefer a scheduled main run every few hours in its own concurrency group if A is not adopted.

  3. CFail fast on lint

    Run npm run lint (3.5 s) as the first step of each test job, or make the shard jobs depend on a short lint job. A lint-failing push then stops within minutes; the trade-off is no test results for that push.

  4. DSession discipline only

    Tell sessions in CLAUDE.md to check gh run list --branch main --workflow CI --limit 1 before pushing and to wait for their own run before merging. Already asked for today and followed by 5% of merges.

Impact

A removes most of the 27,057 runner-minutes a week spent re-failing a broken base and keeps main green by construction; C saves ~5,400 more. Merges would wait ~22 minutes plus queue instead of ~3 minutes, which is acceptable only once BT-01 brings the queue down; with both, weekly demand could fall by roughly half.

Risk

The risk is throughput, not correctness: with today's p90 queue of 3.5 hours, required checks would stall the agent fleet, so sequence after or with BT-01. Two individually green PRs can still break main together; a periodic main run (option B's schedule) or a merge queue (organization-owned repository) covers that. Nothing here changes what the tests check or where they run.

BT-03Typecheck builds 11 programs that each re-check the same source; one Node program does it in 137 s instead of 483 sPerformanceSimplificationEffort SLow riskHigh confidence
Where
  • package.json:23
  • tsconfig.base.json:1
  • packages/contracts/package.json
  • packages/coordinator/tsconfig.json:3
  • apps/desktop/tsconfig.json:6
  • .github/workflows/ci.yml:53
Evidence

Every internal package sets "types": "./src/index.ts", and npm run typecheck runs tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit per workspace, sequentially. Each program therefore re-parses and re-checks its dependencies' source.

  • CI checks log, run 42386846699 (ubuntu-latest): adapter-claude 18.4 s, adapter-codex 18.6, adapter-opencode 18.6, client 83.4, confined-tools 16.5, contracts 18.9, coordinator 77.1, engine 30.2, providers 17.1, voice 16.6, desktop 41.1; 356 s in all (median 8.8 min over 40 green runs, the largest step in the 11.5-minute checks job).
  • Locally: voice (757 lines of its own) took 32.1 s and built 897,673 types; contracts alone 963,015 types and 4.27 M instantiations; the seven small workspaces each 26-33 s and ~1.7 GB. The ten non-client programs sum to 483 s.
  • A single scratch tsconfig including exactly those ten workspaces' current include sets (types: ["node"], same base options) typechecked in 137.0 s, 4.46 GB peak, 0 errors.
  • TypeScript 7.0.2 (stable since 2026-07-08) on the same combined program: 34.9 s wall (108.8 s CPU over 4 threads), 6.5 GB peak, 2 errors, both the test union in BT-04. Per workspace: client 36.8 s vs 146.4 s, desktop 30.3 vs 75.3, coordinator 38.2 vs 135.0. Contracts and voice report 1,069 and 169 errors under TS 7 because TS 6+ defaults types to an empty list (Cannot find name 'process').
Why it matters

The typecheck is the longest step in the gate and the slowest thing a contributor runs locally (~10.5 minutes measured here), and CLAUDE.md asks for it after every last test edit. Over 70% of the Node-side work is the same files checked again.

Options
  1. ATwo programs: all Node workspaces in one, the client in the otherRecommended

    Add a root tsconfig.node.json listing each Node workspace's current include set (desktop keeps types: ["node"] by setting it for the whole program) and keep the client's tsconfig. Run both in parallel in CI (two background tsc processes need ~8 GB on a 16 GB runner). Keep per-workspace typecheck scripts for focused local use and add a small test that every workspace's include globs appear in the combined config, the way ci-test-plan.test.mjs guards shards.

  2. BProject references with cached build info

    composite projects and tsc -b give incremental local runs and let consumers read contracts' declarations instead of its source. Contracts would need declaration emit of zod-inferred types (large, slow to emit) or isolatedDeclarations, which means annotating ~2,000 exported schemas. L effort.

  3. CAdopt TypeScript 7 for the gate

    Install typescript@7 under an alias for typecheck while keeping 5.9 for dts-bundle-generator (the engine build uses the TS JS API). Requires "types": ["node"] in tsconfig.base.json and fixing the 2 complexity errors; memory rises to 5-6.5 GB per program. A further ~4x after A.

  4. DRun today's 11 programs in parallel

    Halves wall clock on a 4-core runner but not CPU, and memory (1.7-3.6 GB each) limits parallelism to about three.

Impact

A: CI typecheck from 356 s to ~85-100 s (two programs side by side; the Node one comparable to today's coordinator check), the checks job from a median 11.5 minutes to ~4-5 with BT-06 (~6-7 runner-minutes per run, ~2,500 a week); local npm run typecheck from ~10.5 to ~4.5 minutes sequential or ~2.5 parallel. A+C: about 1-1.5 minutes locally. Estimates scale the local combined/sum ratio (0.28) onto CI's per-workspace times.

Risk
